The Bronze Age collapse is typically imagined as a fiery apocalypse of burning palaces and clashing chariot warriors, with the mysterious Sea Peoples descending upon the coasts of the eastern Mediterranean like a tsunami of bronze and flame. We picture the last night of Troy, the smoking ruins of Ugarit, the desperate letters of a Hittite king begging for grain. But there is another way to understand this catastrophe, one that is far less cinematic and far more consequential for the ordinary women and men who actually lived through it. If we are honest about what the archaeological and textual record tells us, we must confront a counterintuitive truth: the Bronze Age collapse was, above all, a bureaucratic failure. The people who suffered the most were not soldiers but clerks, not warriors but the women who received their daily rations of barley from a scribe’s clay tablet. The real weapon that killed them was not a sword or a spear, but the sudden, catastrophic unravelling of administrative systems of storage, redistribution, and accounting. To understand why the collapse mattered to ordinary people—why it mattered so much that it still shapes our own assumptions about civilization—we have to stop staring at the flaming ramparts and look instead at the humble granary ledger.

The Late Bronze Age palatial economies of the Aegean and Near East were not simply centers of elite display or military command. They were, at their core, massive redistributive machines. In Mycenaean Greece, the palace at Pylos, for example, did not exist to crown kings or stage epic poetry. It existed to manage the flow of barley, wheat, olives, figs, wine, livestock, and textiles, as well as the labor of the thousands of people who produced them. We know this because of the Linear B tablets—sun-dried clay records that survived fire, ironically, because the same destruction that ended the palaces accidentally baked their inventories into permanence. These tablets are not exalted literature. They are the tedious paperwork of a complex economy: lists of shepherds and their flocks, allocations of bronze to smiths, counts of rowers, and—most tellingly—rations for what the tablets call “women of the household” and their children. These women, many of them probably captives or laborers in textile workshops, received fixed quantities of grain and figs in exchange for their work. And they were not alone. Across the palatial world, from Knossos to Mycenae to Thebes, the system functioned like a vast corporate enterprise: the palace collected surplus from farmers and pastoralists, stored it in vast magazines containing pithoi jars as tall as a woman, and then redistributed it as wages, rations, and emergency relief.

This is where the story turns ordinary. For the common farmer who did not live on an estate, the palace was not an abstract symbol of power. It was the place where he brought his tithe of wheat and from which, in a bad year, he could draw seed grain or emergency supplies. The palace granaries were, in effect, a social safety net. When a drought failed the crops, when a raiding party burned a village’s own granary, when a disease killed the livestock, the people did not turn to kinsmen or local lords first—they turned to the central storage. The administrative records show that the palaces kept surpluses specifically to support workers during the lean months. A tablet from Knossos lists rations for a group of 300 “men of the workshops” receiving sixty liters of wheat each, a precise and generous daily allowance for active males. Similar tablets from Pylos detail rations for twenty-five women and fifteen children at a place called “Ro-u-so,” a small community. This is not ancient welfare ideology; it is boring, functional bookkeeping. But it was precisely this boring bookkeeping that kept ordinary people alive in times of stress. The palace was an insurance policy written in clay.

Now consider what happened when the system collapsed. The palaces burned, and with them went the only records that told administrators how much grain was in store, how many people were owed rations, and when the next distribution would occur. But the loss of records was not merely an intellectual problem. The granaries themselves were destroyed. At Pylos, the excavators found the Linear B tablets in the burning destruction level of the palace, alongside the skeletal remains of the final occupants. The palace magazines were consumed by fire, the pithoi cracked and toppled, their contents turned to charcoal. Within days of that fire, the carefully calibrated redistribution network—which had connected thousands of laborers, shepherds, smiths, and farmers across the region—ceased to exist. The women who had received their daily barley ration in exchange for grinding grain or weaving cloth suddenly found that no one was counting their work anymore. And that was the worst news possible. Because without the palace’s central granary, no other institution in the region had the scale to store surplus or the authority to distribute it. The ordinary people of Pylos did not die from an enemy spear thrust. They died, over the ensuing months, from starvation, from opportunistic disease, from the inability to coordinate a basic harvest without the administrative scaffolding that had made large-scale agriculture possible.

This is the essence of the collapse that gets lost in the epic retellings: the fragility that ordinary people experienced was not a fragility of weaponry but of complex interdependence. The late Bronze Age economy functioned because of a vast, transnational supply chain that moved tin from Afghanistan or Cornwall, copper from Cyprus, ivory from Africa, and grain from the Anatolian plateau to the Aegean coast. The palaces were the nodes that coordinated these flows. When those nodes were destroyed—whether by raiders, internal revolt, or the cascading effects of climate-driven famine—the entire web unraveled. The result was not a return to a simpler, more pastoral life. It was a demographic catastrophe. Across Greece, population declined by as much as seventy-five percent in the centuries after 1200 BCE. Coastal settlements were abandoned for inland villages. Writing disappeared, not because people forgot how to write, but because the administrative need for writing vanished—there was no longer a central bureaucracy to keep records, so there was no longer a reason to scratch marks into clay. The ordinary people who survived did so by abandoning the very complexity that had once protected them. They reverted to subsistence farming, herding sheep, and living in small, isolated hamlets with no central authority, no granary, no safety net.

Now I want you to think about what that meant for a specific ordinary person: a woman named, let us say, “A-pu-wa,” who appears in a Pylos tablet as a “sweeper” in the sanctuary, receiving a small ration of figs and barley. Under the palatial system, her life was hard—she worked, she was fed, and she had no other options. But she did not go hungry while her employer stood. When the palace burned, did she pick up a sword? Of course not. She picked up a basket and tried to find wild grain or acorns. The collapse did not suddenly free her from an oppressor; it abandoned her to a world without infrastructure. Her survival depended on the very structures that historians often dismiss as merely exploitative. The exploitation was real, but so was the security. And here is the uncomfortable lesson: for the bottom tier of society, the loss of a complex system almost always hits harder than the system’s own injustices. The people who study the Bronze Age collapse often focus on the fall of kingdoms, the rise of iron technology, or the origins of the Homeric epics. But the ordinary person’s experience was much more prosaic—and much more devastating. They lost their safety net, their access to metal tools (since bronze production depended on the same trade networks that collapsed), their ability to repair a plow, their knowledge of how to weave a large cloth, their very social forms of belonging.

Her life under the palatial system is hard work, but she's fed, she's housed, she has nowhere else to go. She wouldn't starve while the palace owners enjoyed their meals. Once the palace is burned down, does she pick up a weapon? No. She gathers some dry stalks and tries to forage for wild grains or nuts. The burning of the palace doesn't liberate her from cruel masters. It leaves her alone in a world without any infrastructure. She endures only because of the very things that historians tend to view as oppressive. She is exploited, yes, but she is also protected. And that is a sobering thought: when a complex society collapses, the people at the bottom pay the highest price. The injustice of the system is less severe than the loss of the social safety net, the loss of access to the equipment necessary to sustain life (the procurement of bronze depended upon the very same international trade network), the loss of the ability to repair or construct items, the loss of the expertise required to create them, the loss of the sense of community one shared with others.

Storage: The palace at Pylos had a large storage facility, at what is called the Southeast Building, where we have found evidence of olive oil production and of the distillation of perfume.

The Bronze Age collapse has always been imagined as a dramatic apocalyptic event: the burning palace, the clash of chariot warriors on the battlefield, the mysterious Sea Peoples sweeping up onto the shores of the eastern Mediterranean like a storm wave of metal and fire. It is the final night of the city of Troy, the ruins of Ugarit, a Minoan king’s letter pleading for food.

There is, however, a much more mundane but perhaps equally significant interpretation of this collapse, one that reflects the daily lives of regular men and women who lived during this time. If we are to truthfully represent what our archaeological and textual records can tell us, we must come to terms with a surprising fact: the Bronze Age collapse was above all a failure of bureaucracy. The primary victims of the collapse were not the warriors, but the graffiti-writers and the ordinary women who received their daily provision of barley from a scribe's tablet of clay.

The fatal blow they had to endure came not from weapons, but from the collapse of a highly organized system of storage, distribution, and accounting.

So, to understand why the Bronze Age collapse affected normal men and women so profoundly — and how it influenced our current understanding of what constitutes civilization — we must look away from the burning walls and at the humble ledger kept in a storehouse.

The Late Bronze Age palatial economies of the Aegean and Near East were not simply nuclei of power, wealth and military strength. They were rather great circulation systems for goods and knowledge. The Mycenaean palace at Pylos was not built to glorify monarchs or compose poetry. It was built to organize the movement of barley, wheat, olive oil, olives, figs, wine, animals, cloth, and the workforce that produced all these items. We know this thanks to Linear B tables — mud tablets with scribbled texts, which were preserved by the fire, paradoxically, since the very destruction of the palaces fired them to eternity.

They are not high art, but paper and pen work of a very precise economic system: registers of flocks under individual shepherds, distributions of copper to artisans, inventories of oars and men, but most significantly provisions for the “slave girls of the house” and their children. The latter were most likely prisoners or workers at textile mills, and they were supplied with set amounts of grain and figs as payment for their labor.

And again, they were not the only ones. Palaces in Knossos, in Mycenae, in Thebes were no different from any other modern company: they took goods from producers, held them in great magazines made of floor to roof pitchers, and paid workers a wages, food or a reserve fund in case of a crisis.

It seems obvious now. For the ordinary farmer who did not work on the kings’ estates, this palace was just another place around which he had to circle to give his tithe of grain and get back seed or relief in case of bad harvest. The granaries were a form of insurance. When there was no crop, when the enemy burned down the local granary, when a plague struck home, the people didn’t seek help from their kin or local patron, but from the palace. The accounts of the palatial bureaucracy make it clear that the reserves were intended to keep workers fed when production dropped to a minimum.

A document from Knossos shows rations for 300 ‘workshop workers’, 60 litres of wheat for each — a huge average for an adult worker. Other tablets from Pylos list rations for 25 women and 15 kids at a place called ‘Ro-u-so’. This isn’t just welfare policy; it’s day-to-day bureaucracy. But this bureaucracy was what preserved the lives of ordinary people. The palace was an insurance policy made of parchment.

And then came the collapse. The palaces were burned and all the information about how much grain was stored, who was entitled to what, and when the next shipment would arrive, was lost. And this wasn’t the end of the matter. The palaces’ food magazines were also destroyed. Excavators in Pylos discovered the Linear B tablets amidst the ruins of the last days of the palace building, buried with the bones of the last living people there.

The magazines had been burned, the pithoi jars smashed and overturned, their contents charred. Soon after this destruction, the supply chain, which had sustained thousands of people, stopped working. The women who once received their daily share of barley as payment for milling grain or spinning thread now had nothing to exchange. And that was the worst part of all. Without the palace’s great vaults there was no place in the region with the capacity to hold surplus grain or the authority to distribute it.

The commoners of Pylos didn’t perish at the hands of invading charioteers. Over the course of several months, they starved. They contracted illnesses they should have been protected from. They couldn’t organize a harvest because there was no way to distribute it. This is the real story of the collapse, the one that’s never in the books: the vulnerability of ordinary people isn’t in weapons or armor, but in their inability to function within a system that supports them.

The late Bronze Age economy worked because of a massive, multinational, and cross-regional trade network. Tin was shipped from Afghanistan or Cornwall to meet demand in the Aegean. Copper came from Cyprus. Ivory was imported from Africa. Grain was supplied from the Anatolian plateau.

Palatial administrations functioned to regulate these flows. When those palaces were destroyed — by attack, rebellion, or the effects of climate driven famine — the whole structure fell apart. You don’t revert to a pastoral economy. You experience a population crash. The populations of the coastal areas shrank by up to seventy-five per cent in the few centuries after 1200 BCE. Places along the coast disappeared, replaced by inland villages. Writing was lost, but not because they forgot how to write, but because the need to write had disappeared. There was no more central authority that needed to record its business activities, so why bother to scratch a mark in the clay?

The people who survived don’t use tools they used before. They become farmers. They herd animals. They live in small villages. They don’t build granaries. There is no social organisation. There is no politics. There is no rule of law.

I’d like to ask you to imagine a real person, an everyday woman, called, perhaps, ‘A-pu-wa’, and see what happened to her. She shows up on a Linear B tablet from Pylos, and is listed as a ‘sweeper’ at the temple, with a small allotment of figs and barley as pay. Her life under the palace regime was not great. She did the work that needed doing, and she might not have seen much for it, but it was enough to keep her going, and to feed her on the days when she didn’t work.

But the palace burned. Did she take up a sword? No, she took a basket and foraged for acorns and wild grain. The collapse didn’t give her a chance to get revenge on an enemy. She was left alone in an environment without structure. She could survive thanks to the very things that scholars would say were abuses of power. The abuse was there, but the protection was there, too. Here’s the problem: the least powerful members of society will suffer the most when a complex system falls.

The arguments about the collapse of the Bronze Age are usually based on a discussion of the collapse of kingdoms, the invention of iron, or the Homeric poems. The everyday person experienced a very different set of problems. They lost the protection of a safety net. They lost access to metal tools, which are essential to ploughing (since bronze depended on the trade networks that were destroyed), and to fixing their ploughs, and they lost the ability to make large textiles. They lost their way of life.

There is the matter of storage. At Pylos the palatial system included a large, centralised storage site, known as the ‘South-East Building’, where olive oil and perfumes were made in significant quantities.

Think of the Bronze Age Collapse and what image is the first thing that pops into your head? Pyramids exploding, war chariots crashing into each other, waves upon waves of unknown warriors, the Sea Peoples, descending upon the coasts of the eastern Mediterranean Sea.

You can picture the final night of Troy, the ruined city of Ugarit, the letters of a Hittite king begging again and again for wheat. There’s another way to think about this era, however, perhaps a more grounded way. A way that gives us something of real value, something we might care about.

If you believe the archaeological and textual records then yes, I’m afraid that the Bronze Age Collapse had very little to do with warfare, and a great deal to do with the breakdown of palace management. Those who suffered the most were not the generals, but the accountants; not the warriors, but the women who collected their scribes’ daily ration of barley from a tablet. The weapon here was not a sword, not a spear, but the sudden breakdown of storage, distribution and tracking. To understand why the Collapse mattered to the average person – I mean really, why it still matters today – we need to look away from the ruins of buildings and towards a common barn ledger.

The palaces of the Late Bronze Age in the Aegean and the Near East were not just trading centres for impressing on enemies and glorifying rulers, but rather systems built on administrative mechanisms to be able to handle vast amounts of food.

The palace at Pylos in Mycenaean Greece was not designed to celebrate a king, and certainly not to inspire passages from the Iliad, but designed to control the storage and distribution of grain, grain, olives, figs, wine, animals and textiles, and to monitor the efforts of hundreds, maybe thousands, of the individuals behind them.

The clay tablets which recorded these activities were baked by the fire that consumed the palace. It might seem strange that the tablets survived, but it was because they survived that they can now explain how the palace worked. And this is not a story of bravery and heroic figures, but instead a tale of the banality of numbers, of accountants and the individuals they managed.

Lists of which sheep belonged to which sheep-herder, how much gold was meant to go to one of the city smiths, how many rowers could be drawn from the city navy for defense, and most critically of all, how much food a particular family consisting of several women and some of their children were meant to receive.

A great many of these women were hostages or slaves or indentured, who worked in textile workshops. A similar pattern can be found elsewhere in the palatial world, in Knossos, Mycenae and Thebes: the unit of production in the area is centralised; large quantities of surplus grain are taken from farmers and herdsmen, and then returned in exchange for work.

Here is the ordinariness of the collapse: for the non-aristocratic farmer, the palace was not an idea or a great person, but rather the place to deposit grain, and the place in times of trouble to seek seed corn or emergency food. The storage facilities of the palace were effectively a welfare system.

When drought, raiders or disease came along, destroying the farmer’s stores or killing his livestock, the people didn’t go to friends or family, or eventually to a local lord. Instead, they went to the central storage facilities.

The records show that the palaces maintained emergency reserves of goods, during periods where employees received pay, or not at all. We see in a single tablet at Knossos an inventory of the supplies given to a group of 300 workshop employees. Thirty of them get sixty (litres?) of wheat a day, for a month—a very generous daily ration.

At Pylos, we find a list of the daily rations of twenty-five women and fifteen children given to the twenty-five members of the Ro-u-so workshop.

This isn't ancient welfare legislation, it’s not history, and it’s not poetry. It’s boring, mundane accountancy. But that boring, mundane accountancy is what kept this group of people alive in times of crisis. The palace provided a form of insurance for everyone, written in clay.

And now imagine how things looked after the collapse. The palaces were burned to the ground and the inscriptions falling into the dust: nothing remained for the officials to record the quantities of stored food, to calculate the debt owed by the palace, or to predict when they’d be able to fulfil their payments. But the loss of inscriptions was never going to be the only problem. The granaries of the palaces had also been destroyed.

Archaeologists excavated the Linear B tablets among the debris and remains of the mortal remains of the last inhabitants of the palace at Pylos. The magazines had been burned, the pithoi had been shattered, the contents burned to char and ash. With the days of fire the complex network of trade and rations which connected thousands of shepherds, smiths and farmers, and hundreds of others across the region unlinked. The women who previously exchanged their labour for barley saw their work no longer being counted. And there is no greater anguish for a worker than to see that their work is ignored.

There was no other institution around big enough to absorb the grain or distribute it.

The farmers of Pylos did not perish from a soldier stabbing them with a sword. They perished from having no way to organise their own agricultural production. They perished from trying to do things that nobody could have done without a centralised system. That is the kind of collapse that is forgotten in most accounts of the period. The things were not catastrophic weapons, but things of mutual dependence. The economies of the Late Bronze Age survived because there were huge-scale supply lines bringing tin from Afghanistan or Cornwall, copper from Cyprus, ivory from Africa and grain from the Anatolian Highlands to the Aegean coast. The palaces were the links in these chains.

When the links were broken (by raiders, insurrection, or widespread famine induced by climate change), the whole system disintegrated. There was not a shift to a more pastoral lifestyle, but to a demographic catastrophe. Across Greece the population dropped as much as seventy-five percent during the centuries following 1200 BC. Coastal towns replaced by inland villages. Writing fell into abeyance-not because anyone had lost their ability to read but because the administrative function that led to writing was no longer necessary, and so nobody wrote. All the surviving inhabitants had to do was surrender everything they depended on. They went back to farming and raising flocks, or they moved to small settlements that had no link to any kind of central authority. There was no grain storage. There was no social safety net.

Now imagine that you are one of those women, perhaps called A-pu-wa, and you are mentioned in a tablet from Pylos as the person sweeping the temple courtyard who was paid a small amount of figs and barley. With the palace around, your life might have been hard, but at least you didn’t starve while the palace fed you. If the palace is gone, does she pick up a sword? No, she picks up a basket and looks for acorns or wild grains. The collapse did not free her from the constraints of the system, but left her in a situation where there was nothing at all. She was still dependent on the very institutions that we usually dislike in the classroom. And yes, there was exploitation, but there was also protection. Here is where things are uncomfortable: at the bottom end of the spectrum, losing complex systems often feels worse than the system's injustice.

So much of the research on the Age of Bronze Collapse centres around the end of empires, the start of the Iron Age, or the origins of Homer. The truth of the collapse for the average person was far more prosaic, and much more brutal. They lost access to tools and the ability to fix tools. They lost the ability to give, and the ability to beg. They lost the ability to store, to trade, and to understand how to make cloth. They lost community, they lost humanity. Think only about the storage issue.

In the days before the collapse the Pylos region had a major storage facility known as the 'Southeast Building', which stored large quantities of olives and perfumes for refining.

I lay down for a while on a low wall that surrounded a litter-strewn planter in a garden above the North Circular. The great bridge, designed to hide the road beneath, had been turned into a public plaza. Few people stopped here. The fumes rising from below, and the unnatural hum of traffic that permeated their consciousness, seemed to deter them. I was alone with my thoughts for a few minutes, calculating and recalibrating. I was unsure of the destination or manner of the walk’s conclusion. After this pause, all the possible exit points from the route seemed remote and complicated by subsequent travel logistics. I could have ended the journey there, returning to the city to idle lazily for hours. Or I could have continued. Curiosity prevailed. This same peculiar urge, which had largely initiated the walk, drew my attention to Rookery Path across the street. This narrow alleyway, running along the edge of the chasm occupied by the North Circular and guiding pedestrians away from Waitrose, seemed significant enough to warrant its own street name. Naming pathways is not customary practice in Redbridge, suggesting a certain provenance. I wondered how long this route had existed and how far it extended; I needed to ascertain these facts. I began walking steeply downhill along the narrow path. Descents do not suit me; while climbing is exhausting for the lungs and knees, descending requires a degree of balance and the ability to counteract momentum—two attributes I struggle to maintain even at my best. Complicating matters further was a procession of cyclists who appeared determined to ascend the hill as a test of bravery or stamina. They swayed along, their bicycles moving haphazardly beneath them as they leaned their full weight and power onto the pedals, huffing, grimacing, and staring resolutely at a point inches ahead of their front wheels. I dodged and weaved, striving to remain upright and avoid the path of the passing cycles. Eventually, the path leveled out beside the road, sandwiched between a massive concrete wall and more sturdy, grime-streaked chain-link fencing. The road felt merely inches away, and another sobering cluster of browning flowers marked the spot where a casualty had been claimed. A sign urged pedestrians not to cross at this designated accident site. The only direction was forward, passing additional signs confirming that this was Rookery Path. There are few references to Rookery Path beyond what appears to be a news report of the incident commemorated by the flowers I had observed. However, it appears that The Rookery was one of two large, ancient estates divided by George Lane, which now constitutes the main shopping street of South Woodford. This path seems to lack significant historical pedigree; the 1923 Ministry of Transport map displays nothing but whitespace in this area, while later maps chart the proposed route of the Woodford Spur road cutting across open countryside toward the Roding Valley. Today, the re-routed course of this road is buried beneath the A406 as it curves gently southward, with concrete ramps ascending to carry the initial sections of the M11 high over Charlie Brown’s roundabout. My footpath edged around the junction, connecting the ends of cul-de-sacs formed by the interruption of this landscape of overbridges and viaducts. I was eventually committed to a slightly perilous crossing of Chigwell Road in order to pass under the wooden arch marking the entrance to Roding Valley Park. Once again, I found myself on familiar ground.

I was eventually committed to an unconvincing, almost dangerous, cross over Chigwel Road onto the path under the wooden entrance arch to the Roding Valley Park. And once more was found on familiar ground.

So far I am off and I come to a stop on a low wall around a litter strewn planter in a garden on top of the North Circular Road. The once vast bridge that hid this road underneath, has been turned into a public parade ground and few people have the patience to pause for a few moments, the fumes that come out of that hole ruin the level flight of the unnatural hum of traffic, winding in, like opium through their consciousness. I am alone with my thoughts for a few minutes calculating and recalculating, not sure where or how the walk will be brought to an end. A few moments later, all options for an end to the walk seem remote and complicated by travel issues afterwards. I could end it right there and simply go back to town, idle lazily for hours. Or I can go on - curiosity wins and I notice something across the road, the narrow Rookery Path leads along the edge of a now North Circle chasm, currently abandoned for Waitrose. There seems to be something important here to have its own street name, the naming of which is not an activity that Redbridge undertakes very much - there is clearly some provenance there. How long has this been there, how far does it extend, and when will I find out? And off I go, downwards along the narrow path and I can’t get used to walking downhill. Up is tiring for the lungs and knees, but down requires a degree of balance, the ability to check momentum, two things I have very little of even on the best of days. And then there are the cyclists swaying as they need to be squarely up the hill, some test of either their bravery or stamina, huffing and grimacing and aiming their eyes at a point a few inches past the front wheel of the bike shunting negligently beneath them, full weight and power upon the pedals, staring at a point a few inches ahead of the front tyre and I have to dodge wind and weave, trying to stay sideways up and avoid the multiple paths of the passing cycles. Eventually the path levels out alongside the road, in the space between a massive concrete wall and another of more sturdy, but grime striped chain link, the road itself feels merely inches away and another sobering sprinkling of browning flowers mark the place a pedestrian casualty has been issued out of, and a sign telling pedestrians not to cross it at this designated site of violence. There is nowhere except forward past more signs telling me that I am thus far along Rookery Path. There seem to be few references to Rookery Path except what appears to be a news report of the event that got me the flowers I’ve just been staring at. Yet it seems like The Rookery was one of two large old estates that George Lane, the main shopping street of South Woodford now, divided. This path has little pedigree with the old 1923 Ministry of Transport map showing nothing but whitespace here. Later maps show the proposed route of the Woodford Spur road cutting across open countryside in our direction towards the Roding Valley. Today the re-routed course of this road is buried under the A406 as it curves gently south, concrete ramps ascending to take off the initial bits of the M11 high over Charlie Brown’s roundabout, and my footpath edges around this junction, alongside the each end of two cul-de-sacs caused from interrupting this landscape of overbridges and viaducts. Eventually I am committed to a slightly dangerous crossing of Chigwell Road, to progress under the wooden arch of the entrance to Roding Valley Park, and once again, I am on familiar ground.

Research shows that AI technology positively affects students’ writing skills. However, this topic has not yet been explored by Indonesian researchers. Therefore, this study aims to map perceptions, obstacles, and recommendations for optimizing the use of AI in teaching academic writing in Indonesian. This article focuses on a case study of three senior high schools in Central Java, Indonesia. The research method used is a mixed method approach, using both quantitative and qualitative data. Data collection was carried out using questionnaires with Likert scales, followed by in-depth interviews using mobile instant messaging. The findings of this study are: (1) AI-based learning tools help students in academic research, especially in the planning stage for identifying and developing topics, and in the drafting stage for creating paper drafts; (2) AI-based learning tools are considered flexible in terms of accessibility, although they do not fully address all student needs throughout the writing process; (3) students are interested in using AI technology in academic writing classes to prevent the learning process from becoming monotonous. Despite the integration of AI into academic writing classes, the tools have not positively impacted the quality of students’ academic papers across all indicators. Several obstacles to using AI were identified, including the need for more available features, especially for editing Indonesian text, and the necessity to optimize existing features. Therefore, this study recommends adding features to edit Indonesian text, including spelling, diction, and sentence structure, as well as enhancing AI literacy to enable the optimal exploration and leverage of existing features. Finally, this research did not account for the verification of the originality and accuracy of written products assisted by AI-based learning tools, which could serve as a focus for future researchers.

Days and weeks rolled past in a trice, and still he lived on the cabbage-trees, and then on frogs and snakes, and whatever else he could find, and all was welcome and savory to him. But he grew more and more emaciated, till he could scarcely crawl. At length, after forty days, by his own reckoning, he reached the river bank. His clothes were in rags, his once bright axe was rusted, his face was hidden by a beard, his hair was matted, his feeble frame was little more than a skeleton covered with parchment, and there he lay down to die. In the disturbed dreams of his fevered imagination, he thought he heard the distant noise of oars on the silent river. He listened, but the sounds were gone from his hearing. It was a dream, the last gleam of expiring hope, and the light of life was about to be extinguished forever. But the sound of oars awoke him from his lethargy once more. He listened, and even the hum of a fly could not have escaped his ear. They were indeed the measured beats of oars, and to the forlorn soul it was a moment of joy. The sound of human voices thrilled his heart, and awakened the tumultuous pulses of returning hope. The eye of God saw that poor man on his knees by the broad, still stream that glittered in the sunbeams, and human eyes soon saw him also. A little boat, propelled by its vigorous rowers, boldly advanced around the headland covered with tangled brushwood. The Lost One raised his feeble voice in a loud, shrill scream of joy and fear. The rowers paused and looked around. At another, though feebler, scream, they observed him. As the boat approached, his heart fluttered, his sight dimmed, his brain reeled, and he gasped for breath. The boat ran upon the beach, and the Lost One was found.

Days; days; weeks—they came thick on each other. Food—food—what there was, first he ate of the cabbage trees; then of frogs and snakes-he was welcome to it all; all was savoury. And yet, such was not his hunger, that, notwith¬standing all this food, he grew thinner and thinner till he could scarse crawl, and, after forty days by his own reckoning, came to the bank of the river, in a wretched stripe of tatters, his bright axe abraded and rusty, his face bearded, his hair tufted, his feeble frame just a skeleton covered with parchment—there he lay down to die. Here, too, amid the dreams of his fevered imagination, was brought to him the far-off noise of oars on the meatless river; and he attended it, but they faded from his ear. It was that which the dying man felt,—an only weak speck of a dream,—dying hope, which was too faint to be felt,—a light about to be quenched for ever, That which made to stun his ear—the oar awoke him again, and he listened with such an eager ear, that the hum of a fly might have reached it. Thank you Jorge. Global digital cooperation is at a critical juncture. The benefits of connectivity are unevenly distributed, and digital exclusion, including the gender digital gap, prevents many people from fully realizing the benefits of the digital revolution. Social and economic injustices are an urgent challenge to development and democracy. To achieve the Agenda 2030 and ensure that the Global Digital Compact contributes to it, bold and committed actions are required. The benefits of digitalization must be extended to all countries and people. Digital resources must be governed in a transparent, inclusive, and accountable manner, protecting the public core of the internet. Digital policies and laws must be designed to catalyze meaningful innovation. A definitive paradigm shift is necessary to address the paradox of digital inequality. As connectivity expands, digital inequality is amplified because all technologies converge into the broader phenomenon of digitalization. The threat that the digital revolution will bypass developing countries is becoming increasingly real. This issue extends beyond mere internet access; it encompasses the complex challenges of access quality, affordability, and the equal participation of nations in the global regimes that establish the rules of engagement. People everywhere require the skills necessary to seize the opportunities presented by this new paradigm. It is paramount to bridge the gap between those who possess the technological and financial resources to use the internet and other digital technologies for transaction, prosperity, and national wealth creation, and those who do not. Powerful nations frequently utilize free trade agreements to undermine the digital rights of peoples and countries, particularly in the Global South. Trade rules are employed to coerce governments into hyper-liberalizing data flows, thereby stripping local public authorities of their autonomy to govern transnational entities. Monopoly corporations and their algorithms prevent the scrutiny of source code and legitimize a permanent dependence of developing countries on entities that control data and artificial intelligence power. This infrastructural dependence is equivalent to a neo-colonial, extractivist order. The unfinished business of the World Summit on the Information Society (WSIS) must not be forgotten. This historical context underscores the importance of the WSIS and the necessity for the Global Digital Compact to address the technologies that have emerged over the last two decades. It is essential to establish political, regulatory, technical, and financial conditions that enhance the individual and collective agency, autonomy, and choice of people in connecting to digital technologies and spaces. Additionally, these conditions must ensure that people retain their right to vote and participate in the democratic process. The WSIS provides a foundation based on human rights, as well as intersectional and feminist frameworks, to address the geopolitics of global inequality and injustice. Ultimately, the conclusive test of a well-guided digital transition lies in the public, collective, and social value it creates, and the human freedoms it expands.

Growth in 3rd Area of Growth: Information and Communication Technology (ICT)

In the classroom, we have tried using different digital tools to help students gain access to and participate in learning. Digital tools we have used include presentations, iPads, Videos, Emoji input, and a virtual field trip to Mango Lake. These digital tools have been especially helpful to the students who were calmly inclined and those with reading comprehension difficulties because they helped to reduce the demand on the students, allowing them more opportunities to engage and connect. In the clinic, we have used ICT mainly to provide various pieces of information, rather than using ICT as an independent source of information.

The ACARA definition of the competence criterion “critical and creative thinking” states that students can identify, process, and evaluate information from many different sources, including the reliability and validity of those sources and how they evaluate relevance and utility. Likewise, the NSW Critical Thinking report asserts that in the context of increasingly available digital information, “assessing sources and reading across texts are central to long-term critical thinking” (Roberts-Hull et al, 2021). Consequently, although we have used technology in our clinic, we have not always provided students with clear instruction that would assist them in interpreting digital information. Thus, in order to use ICT more purposefully, we should not discard the use of videos or virtual field trips, but add a step of ‘source assessment’. We can ask the students questions like “Who made this?”, “Why are we making this?”, “What sources were used to make this?”, and “If a person with a different view made this information, would it look different?”

The same direction applies to the future use of AI in the humanities and social sciences: AI results should be viewed as “claims that can be verified” and “not knowledge that saves us from expressing scientific judgments”. Based on these concepts, we have come up with three guiding principles to future lesson planning: First, each teaching unit should concentrate on one central question rather than many interesting but conflicting topics. Second, formative assessments should advance beyond simply confirming ‘students’ memory’ to establishing ‘students’ claims’. Third, when choosing digital resources, we should consider not just their ‘accessibility and attractiveness’, but also their ‘worth investigating as an object of study’.

To be specific, when introducing and summarizing a lesson planning unit, we will continue to repeat the topic and use visuals, and provide a brief ‘assertion-evidence-conclusion’ task as the final task. We will continue to ask calmly inclined students to take part, but we will promote their participation by asking specific questions, giving longer time for responses, providing rehearsal opportunities, and offering sentences to help them build them up. As for the topics related to the indigenous people, we will prepare a planning checklist to check that the resources used are ‘recognized by the community’, ‘as much as possible adapted to the local area’, and ‘presented as living knowledge and not just as old material’.

Student responses to tutor feedback questions, wrong answers on worksheets, and student responses during classroom discussion will be written in a uniform template after class to be reviewed and improved by the class team and mainly focus on improving “the quality of questioning, evidence and assessment strategies”. As our practice shows, a successful history and social studies lesson is not about gathering all the interesting resources; it is about the selective use of content, questions, and forms of inquiry to help students create explanations about the past with the support of historical evidence (Department of Education and Training Victoria, 2020; Hattie & Timperley, 2007; Roberts-Hull, 2021).

Multiple armed groups are active in Oromia and all are accused of committing killings. The forces participating in the government’s operation against the OLA are active throughout Oromia and include the Ethiopian National Defence Forces, federal police, Oromia special forces and police, Amhara special forces, Fano, local militants, anti-terrorist forces, Oromia militia forces, and Gachana Sirna. Gachana Sirna translates to the “shield” or “guardians” of the system. This local security structure was formally established by the Oromia Regional Council in March 2022 to enable residents to protect their local communities from threats. The Gachana Sirna is accountable to the kebele administrator and is monitored, supervised, and supported by the local militia office (a newly established security structure) and the local security council. Members are selected from the local community by kebele administrators and are provided with armaments by the militia office. One of the stated duties of the Gachana Sirna is to track down and verify the identity of individuals who are not residents of the neighborhood and to inform the concerned parties. Local government reports suggest their active involvement in fighting against the OLA in several parts of Oromia since August 2021. Federal Republican Guard forces are active in central Oromia, particularly in areas surrounding the capital. Amhara special forces and militias are active in areas bordering the Amhara region, particularly in the East Shewa Zone. The OLA, government forces, an alleged regime-allied OLA clone, Amhara Fano, local militias, and other unidentified armed groups maintain an active presence in Oromia, particularly in Wollega. The government is also accused of organizing and deploying parallel armed groups similar to the OLA and the anti-regime assassin group known as Abbaa Torbee. Abbaa Torbee is a semi-legendary assassin who, after issuing warnings, is said to have executed rogue officials that were obstructing the Oromo protests between 2014 and 2018. Some residents of Oromia believe that these parallel armed forces commit crimes in an attempt to decimate the OLA’s credibility and turn the Oromo public against its insurgency.

The strip of scrubby, litter-strewn land between the New River and the Great Cambridge Road looked forlorn and derelict. I was allowed to use it only by the sufferance of the British Province of the Society of Jesus, but the notice on the permissive footway had been defaced to remove the last word, giving the illusion of a mysterious secret society in this unlikely location. This land adjoins the well-tended grounds of St. Ignatius’ College, a Jesuit school, but the course of the Brook remains largely wild and untouched, presumably on land stockpiled for the future expansion of a school deemed ‘good’ by OfSTED. From the crossing of the New River, the swish and drone of the road ahead was audible, and the long walk through quiet suburban parks made this noise seem alien and unwelcome. Between the overgrown edges of the path ahead, the silver flash of hubcaps was visible against the grimy, standard-issue anti-pedestrian fencing of the road’s median. The path abruptly terminated onto flagstones at the foot of a steep staircase leading to a footbridge, while cyclists were diverted to the south in pursuit of an underpass some distance away. As I clambered to the peak of the slender bridge, swaying gently under the weight of holding me above the traffic, I observed the impressively broad dual-carriageway below. This was ancient Ermine Street, the Roman road to Lincoln and York. It had begun its journey in the heart of the City of London, sluggishly pressing through the traffic of Dalston and Tottenham, edging along the wide, flat bottom of the Lea Valley, and patiently awaiting its moment of escape. Suddenly, at Bruce Grove, the road wheels into the suburbs and emerges from the one-way system as a classic 1920s arterial route. It is one of the ‘Great’ roads radiating from London, characterized by modernist factory buildings and large brick villas. However, the ‘Great Cambridge Road’ no longer leads to Cambridge, at least according to the sanctioned destination signs. Only Enfield and Hertford are now name-checked, with no further destinations indicated. Some signs clearly have the old destinations plated over, directing traffic east to the M11, which snakes out to the northeast. Despite this, the old road remains busy and is still the easiest way to escape from east London to the north. Those in the know prefer its long, straight lines to the gently deceptive curves of the motorway. It seems the Romans knew best, as neither time nor transport policy has succeeded in downgrading Ermine Street from its primary route status. I carefully descended from the alarmingly vibrating frame of the bridge and followed the continuation of the path as it burrowed behind the Enfield Crematorium. The route passed a sizeable fringe of the grounds that was not yet used for burials. To the north of the path, a curiously unmarked series of masts, pipes, and generator buildings nestled sinisterly in the undergrowth. I reasoned that these structures likely served an utterly mundane purpose in a state heavy with surveillance of even the least consequential things. The humid air closed in under the overgrown foliage, and the heat and stillness gave the path a malign feeling. This section was part of the London Loop footpath. While I had previously stumbled across and along many sections that were less than salubrious, this was one of the least inviting I had encountered in some time. I was glad to pass under a very low railway bridge and to escape into the open once again near Turkey Street station. A corner of parkland had been recently refurbished to include a circular bench, which was currently in use to support the flowers and photographs of an impromptu memorial. Meanwhile, the brook emerged from under the rails via a solid brick bridge, now flowing along the street with which it shared a name.

S2-glass fiber reinforced plastics (S2-GFRP) and basalt fiber reinforced plastics (BFRP) are important materials because of their excellent mechanical properties. Therefore, milling of these composites plays an important role in achieving the desired properties. However, machining of these materials is difficult due to their relative inhomogeneity compared to metals, leading to unpredictability in milling quality. The main objective of the present study is to investigate the effect of cutting parameters, tool geometry, and tool surface materials on the surface quality of these composites, with burr formation as the key metric. S2-GFRP and BFRP composites were manufactured using the vacuum infusion method. Helical and straight flute end mills were manufactured from high-speed steel (HSS) and carbide blanks. Half of the tools were coated with titanium nitride using reactive magnetron sputtering. A Taguchi L18 orthogonal array was used to determine the effect of tool material, tool angle, coating, cutting direction, spindle speed, and feed rate on the machining quality of S2-GFRPs and BFRPs, specifically with respect to burr formation. Milling experiments were conducted under dry conditions, and the burrs were imaged to calculate the total area and length. Statistical analysis was performed to optimize machining parameters and tool types to ensure the structural integrity and performance of the final composite parts. The results indicate that the selection of tool material has the most significant impact on both the area and length of burrs on the machined surface. Additionally, the novel image analysis technique enables the assessment of burr size extent with desirable operational speed, making it suitable for industrial applications. Key highlights include the manufacturing of aerospace-grade S2-GFRP and BFRP, the fabrication of carbide and HSS end mills with titanium nitride protective coatings, and the machining of FRPs using process parameters designed via the Taguchi method. Notably, distinctive image processing was utilized for the first time to compute milling-induced burr area and length, while statistical analysis was conducted to quantify parameter contributions and optimize the milling process.

PLYMOUTH, a municipal county, parliamentary borough and seaport, in Devonshire, England. It is a city, created in 1888, and extended in 1896, 231 m. west-south-west of London, with a population (1910) of 126,266. It is situated at the head of Plymouth Sound, extending westwards from the river Plym to the mouth of the Tamar, and is separated from the Tamar by the township of East Stonehouse and the borough of Devonport, the three being known collectively as the “Three Towns.” The Prince of Wales is Lord High Steward of the borough. The local government is in the hands of a mayor, 14 aldermen and 42 councillors, and the city is divided into 14 wards. The parliamentary borough returns two members to Parliament, but does not coincide with the municipal borough, as a portion of the latter falls within the Tavistock county division of Devon. The waterfront of the Three Towns consists of Plymouth Sound and its various inlets, which, proceeding from east to west, are the Catwater, Sutton Pool, Mill Bay, Stonehouse Pool and the Hamoaze. High ground flanks the Catwater on the east and the Hamoaze on the west, and there are forts commanding the harbour and its approaches. On the west side of the entrance to the Catwater stands the Citadel, founded in the reign of Henry VIII. and rebuilt by Charles II. The Hoe extends along the northern edge of the Sound, and the view from it includes the rugged Staddon Heights to the east and the wooded slopes of Mount Edgcumbe to the west. To the north the town of Plymouth rises towards the hills known as Mannamead. On the site of an old Trinity House obelisk stands Smeaton’s lighthouse tower, removed from its original position on the Eddystone Reef in 1884, and now used as a wind-recording station in connection with the adjoining Meteorological Observatory. The Hoe has several notable monuments, including a striking statue of Sir Francis Drake by Sir Edgar Boehm, and the Armada Memorial. At the north-east end of the Hoe an obelisk commemorates the troops engaged in the South African War. A municipal bowling green recalls the probable early use of the Hoe. Adjacent to the Citadel, at its south-west angle, is the Marine Biological Station, and further west projects the Promenade Pier. In the Sound is Drake’s Island, formerly St Nicholas’s Island, now strongly fortified. It was once the property of the corporation, and in Stuart times was a place of imprisonment for certain Plymouth Baptist ministers. Few other evidences of the antiquity of the town remain. Below and to the north-east of the Citadel is the Barbican, with a commemorative stone for the “Mayflower.” A considerable fish-buying trade is carried on on the adjacent quay, near which stands the Custom House. From the Barbican winding streets lead past the old Guildhall, built in 1800, which housed the municipal library pending its removal to more commodious quarters in the new museum, opposite the technical and art schools, which are situated in the northernmost part of the town. A short distance to the west stands the new Guildhall, in close proximity to the enlarged post office, central police station, law courts and other municipal buildings. The Guildhall, opened in 1874, is in a bold, rather exotic Early Pointed French style, and its tower at the south-west end rises 190 feet high. It is ornamented with a series of coloured windows depicting events in Plymouth’s history or commemorating men and families connected with the town. The large hall contains a fine organ, and the mayor’s parlour houses a contemporary portrait of Sir Francis Drake and several interesting prints of the town.

The local government is administered by a mayor, 14 aldermen and 42 councillors, the borough being divided into 14 wards. The parliamentary borough returns two members to Parliament, but does not exactly coincide with the municipal borough, as a portion of the latter is within the Tavistock county division of Devon. The waterfront of the “Three Towns” is formed by Plymouth Sound and its inlets, which, proceeding from east to west, are the Catwater, Sutton Pool, Mill Bay, Stonehouse Pool and the Hamoaze. High ground flanks the Catwater to the east and the Hamoaze to the west, and commands the harbour and approaches with forts. On the west side of the entrance to the Catwater stands the Citadel, founded in the reign of Henry VIII., and rebuilt by Charles II. The Hoe extends along the northern edge of the Sound, and its panorama includes the rugged Staddon Heights to the east and the wooded slopes of Mount Edgcumbe to the west. To the north the town of Plymouth rises towards the hills known as Mannamead. On the site of an old Trinity House obelisk stands Smeaton’s lighthouse tower, removed from the Eddystone reef in 1884, and now used as a wind-recording station in connexion with the adjoining Meteorological Observatory. On the Hoe are several notable monuments, including a striking statue of Sir Francis Drake by Sir Edgar Boehm and the Armada Memorial. At the north-east end of the Hoe an obelisk commemorates the troops in the South African War, and a municipal bowling green recalls the probable early use of the Hoe. Adjacent to the Citadel, at its south-west angle, is the Marine Biological Station, and further west projects the Promenade Pier. In the Sound is Drake’s island, formerly St Nicholas’s island, now strongly fortified. It was once the property of the corporation, and in Stuart times was used as a place of imprisonment for certain Plymouth Baptist ministers. Few other evidences of the antiquity of the town remain. Below and to the north-east of the Citadel is the Barbican, with a commemorative stone for the “Mayflower.” A considerable fish-buying trade is carried on on the adjacent quay, near which is the Custom House. From the Barbican winding streets lead past the old Guildhall, built in 1800, which housed the municipal library pending its removal to more commodious quarters in the new museum. This museum is opposite the technical and art schools, situated in the northernmost part of the town. A short distance to the west stands the new Guildhall, in close proximity to the enlarged post office, central police station, law courts and other municipal buildings. Opened in 1874, the Guildhall is built in a bold, rather exotic, Early Pointed French style. Its tower at the south-west end is 190 feet high, and the building is ornamented with a series of coloured windows depicting events in Plymouth’s history or commemorating men and families connected with the town. The large hall contains a fine organ, and the mayor’s parlour has a contemporary portrait of Sir Francis Drake, and several interesting prints of the town.

The Fourth Industrial Revolution has led to a rapid digital transformation in the global business environment, and businesses of all sizes are now required to adopt digital technologies in their operations, products and services. However, large organisations have been more technologically mature and risk-tolerant in adopting digital transformation than SMEs, which often lack the necessary resources and capabilities (Deniz 2021; Morakanyane et al. 2017).

Nevertheless, SMEs in Malaysia and the ASEAN region have increasingly adopted digital platforms in response to changing consumer behaviour due to the widespread use of mobile devices, social media and cloud computing (Peillon and Dubruc 2019). This has significantly changed the way SMEs do business and reach consumers in the digital marketplace. In Malaysia, SMEs form the backbone of the national economy, accounting for around 97.4% of all business establishments and contributing 39.5% to the country’s GDP, or RM652.4 billion in value added (Department of Statistics Malaysia, 2024).

Digital platforms are a new form of economic organisation that has transformed many industries, including retail, transportation and hospitality (Cusumano et al. 2019). For the purpose of this study, we focus on transaction platforms, which facilitate commercial transactions between multiple parties, including sellers, buyers and advertisers (Leong et al. 2023). E-commerce platforms such as Shopee, Lazada and TikTok Shop have become important channels for Malaysian SMEs to reach consumers and sustain commercial activity. In contemporary scholarship and regulatory discourse, these entities are increasingly referred to as ‘Gatekeepers’ because they act as key digital intermediaries that control access to markets, visibility and consumer reach. As such, they may significantly affect the commercial opportunities and viability of SMEs that depend on them.

There is a fundamental difference between how large enterprises and SMEs interact with digital platforms. Large enterprises are generally able to manage their platform relationships from a position of strength, using their extensive internal resources and bargaining power to negotiate favourable terms (Selander et al. 2013). In contrast, SMEs interact with platforms from a position of limited resources and bargaining power, making them more vulnerable to unilateral changes in platform policies, commission rates and algorithmic rankings (Cusumano et al. 2019). This may lead to a form of structural dependency, where SMEs become heavily reliant on dominant digital platforms for market access, business visibility and consumer transactions. It is this condition of digital platform dependency that is the focus of this study and which warrants examination under the Competition Act (CA) 2010.

The fourth industrial revolution has accelerated digital transformation in the business world, where businesses of all sizes must integrate technology in their products and services in order to remain competitive. Because of their greater investment and capability, large corporations are leading SMEs in terms of technological prowess and their willingness to adopt digital transformation amidst SMEs who often struggle with limited resources (Deniz 2021; Morakanyane et al. 2017). Despite this, SMEs in Malaysia and throughout the ASEAN region are beginning to adopt digital platforms in response to changing consumer behaviour driven by the rise in the proliferation of mobile devices, social media, and cloud computing (Peillon and Dubruc 2019). As a result, the ways in which SMEs connect with consumers and market themselves have changed.

Digital platforms are a vital type of economic organisation that has changed many industries, including retail, transportation, and hospitality (Cusumano et al. 2019). This study examines transactional platforms in particular, which allow multiple parties to conduct business, including buyers, sellers, and advertisers (Leong et al. 2023). Recently, e-commerce platforms such as Shopee, Lazada, and TikTok Shop have gained popularity among Malaysian SMEs. These platforms are important because they provide a channel for SMEs to interact with consumers and carry on with their operations. In recent literature and government documents, these platforms are referred to as ‘gatekeepers,’ because they are the digital intermediaries that grant market access, visibility, and consumer reach.

In essence, these platforms may have an impact on the business opportunities available to SMEs. It is worth noting that there is a difference between the way that large corporations and SMEs approach their relation with digital platforms. Large corporations can use a position of strength, given their larger size and larger bargaining power (Selander et al. 2013). On the other hand, SMEs enter into their relationship with platforms from a position of weakness, given their smaller size and smaller bargaining power, thus making them more vulnerable to changes in platform policies, commission rates, and rankings (Cusumano et al. 2019). This could be a form of ‘lock-in’ whereby SMEs depend on platforms to run their businesses. It is this ‘lock-in’ effect that this research intends to investigate from the perspective of the CA 2010.

With the advent of the 4th Industrial Revolution, the global business situation continues to digital increase at a fast pace. Larger organizations show greater technological maturity and are much more proactive about digital transformation at a large scale. SMEs do not have access to the same resources and capabilities that large organizations require (Deniz 2021; Morakanyane et al. 2017). Despite this, between Malaysia and the ASEAN region a growing number of SMEs are moving towards new digital platforms in response to changes in customer behavior caused by mobile phones, social networks and cloud computing (Peillon and Dubruc 2019). This affects the way SMEs manage digitally. In Malaysia, SMEs make up a very large part of the economy. About 97.4 % of all commercial businesses belong to this group and 39.5 % of Malaysia's GDP -or in terms of value added - total RM652.4 billion (Department of Statistics Malaysia, 2024). The digital platform can be seen as a new type of organization for making money and has revolutionized many sectors, such as retail, transport and the hotel industry (Cusumano et al. 2019). Especially transaction platforms, which bring together vendors, customers and advertisers, i.e. companies that make their revenue by processing commercial deals (Leong et al. 2023). Some typical examples in Malaysia are Shopee, Lazada and TikTok Shop, the latter being a very effective means for SMEs to reach customers. By now, these platforms are increasingly being referred to as gatekeepers in industry literature and legal debates because they serve as the main entry point for all the above-mentioned businesses. Thus, gatekeeping can significantly affect the growth and competitive strength of such companies. Both larger companies and SMEs have somewhat different ways of dealing with digital marketplaces. For example, many economies have become large enough to possess internal capabilities in this area (Selander et al. 2013) own resources and significant say in the platform relationship. In negotiated partnership negotiations with platform providers, this means significantly greater control and higher negotiating power (Selander et al. 2013). Smaller companies, on the other hand, usually don't have the same internal capabilities as the big guys and generally haven't as much control and negotiation leverage as the big guys when dealing with platform owners (Selander et al. 2013). For SMEs, smaller companies are more vulnerable to changes in platforms' rules and regulations, service charges and rankings in search results (Cusumano et al. 2019). Therefore, there is a structural dependency that ties SMEs' growth and commercial development to platform partners under platform control. This kind of digital platform dependency is the focus of this study, which examines this within the context of the Interaction of Consumers and Businesses Act 2010 (CA 2010).

From an academic and legislative perspective, platforms are being recognized as "gatekeepers" since they are the primary providers of digital services that control access to the market, discoverability by consumers, and geographical reach of their users. Thus, they can have a significant impact on SMEs' ability to access the market. Small Businesses and large businesses use digital platforms differently.

Generally, large businesses have the resources and bargaining power to dominate the platform and protect their competitive advantage, while SMEs have limited resources and bargaining power and are therefore susceptible to changes in terms of platform policies, commission structures and search algorithms (Killusumano et al., 2019)

This could result in a unique type of structural dependency, where SMEs are increasingly dependent on large platforms as their main means to access the market for consumers, and gaining visibility and generating consumer transactions. This state of dependence on digital platforms is what we will be analyzing in this paper under the 2010 Competition Act (CA).

Our final recommendation for the Global Ethical Investment Fund (GEIF) is as follows:

Based on GEIF’s primary screening criteria, which prioritize SDG alignment, ethical transparency, and genuine performance over greenwashing, we do not recommend outright inclusion in GEIF’s flagship high-conviction ESG funds at this stage. Instead, we recommend placing Air New Zealand on a Conditional Investment Watchlist.

Why this conditional stance? First, from a screening perspective, Air New Zealand does not commit outright fabrication. The company demonstrates commendable operational transparency by publishing detailed emissions data and disclosing its project delays. However, replacing its SBTi-validated 2030 target with non-binding internal guidance introduces a serious 'greenrinsing' risk. Furthermore, while its SDG 12 waste initiatives are positive, they remain localized operational wins rather than systemic, enterprise-wide circularity.

Rather than disinvesting completely, GEIF should utilize an active stewardship approach by setting three mandatory engagement conditions before capital allocation:

Re-commit to a validated science-based target (SBTi) rather than relying on flexible internal guidance.

Establish company-wide, standardized circularity metrics that cover the entire waste footprint—including inflight biosecurity waste.

Provide binding contractual proof of 2030 SAF offtake agreements.

If these conditions are met, Air New Zealand can transition into GEIF's primary portfolio.

In conclusion, Air New Zealand represents a classic case study in hard-to-abate sectors. The company is taking substantive steps toward sustainability, but its current narrative remains slightly ahead of its verified, system-wide delivery.

For an institutional investor like GEIF, championing sustainability means looking beyond polished marketing to demand rigorous, independently verified metrics. By holding companies accountable to science-based standards and complete operational transparency, ethical funds can drive genuine systemic change rather than settling for selective progress.

Thank you for your time. We welcome any questions from the GEIF investment committee.
