The Meiji Restoration and the Art of National Transformation

In the course of a single generation, Japan went from a weak, isolated island nation on the edge of the world to a modern industrial power capable of defeating the Russian Empire in war. The Meiji Restoration of 1868 is often portrayed as a dramatic turning point in Japanese history, but its broader significance is that it is one of the best examples of how a society can intentionally transform itself in response to external pressure and rapid global change. Today, when governments, businesses, and institutions are undergoing their own convulsive transformations due to technology, demographics, and shifting geopolitics, the Meiji experience is worth studying. It reminds us that successful transformation is not a matter of enthusiasm or slogans, but of disciplined sequencing, strategic openness, and the patient construction of capable institutions.

The problem of survival

The restoration was born of a perceived existential threat. For over two hundred years, the Tokugawa shogunate had maintained a policy of limited foreign engagement, controlling trade and restricting contact with the outside world. By the mid-nineteenth century, that arrangement had become dangerously brittle. Western powers, armed with industrial technology and imperial ambitions, were pressing on the region. The arrival of Commodore Perry’s “black ships” in 1853 exposed the fundamental weakness of Japan’s defenses. The elites who overthrew the shogunate understood that the old order could not withstand this new reality. Their goal was not simply to replace a government but to secure Japan’s survival as an independent nation.

This starting point matters. The Meiji leaders did not begin with a romantic vision of modernizing at all costs. They began with a hard assessment of vulnerabilities. They recognized that modernization was not optional; it was a condition for continued sovereignty. Today, organizations and nations face similar moments of reckoning. Technological disruption, supply chain fragility, climate risk, and shifts in the global balance of power can make old institutions obsolete almost overnight. The lesson is neither panic nor denial, but rather an honest inventory of weaknesses. Sustainable transformation begins with acknowledging the gap between current capacity and future demand.

Strategic borrowing, not imitation

One of the most striking features of the Meiji Restoration was its approach to foreign knowledge. The leadership did not attempt to copy any single country wholesale. Instead, they studied multiple models and selected elements that fit Japanese conditions. The legal system drew inspiration from France and Germany; the navy was closely associated with British naval practice; education was influenced by American and European ideas; and constitutional architecture borrowed from Prussian models of strong executive authority. This was not passive imitation but deliberate adaptation.

The Meiji approach embodied a profound intellectual discipline: to treat external models as resources to be tested, not as blueprints to be revered. In an age when best practices travel instantly across borders, the temptation is to import innovation wholesale—a new technology platform, a management framework, a policy design from a high-performing country. Yet transplantation without context rarely succeeds. What made Japan’s borrowing effective was the presence of serious institutional intermediaries—bureaucrats, engineers, educators, and military officers—who translated foreign ideas into local practice. They engaged in what we might now call capacity building: investing in the people and organizations that would operate the new systems. The lesson for contemporary leaders is clear: external ideas are useful only when accompanied by the local capability to adapt, operate, and improve them.

Institutions before infrastructure

A widespread but misleading image of the Meiji Restoration is that of a nation suddenly building railways, factories, and telegraph lines. The physical infrastructure was indeed spectacular, but it was not the foundation. The foundation was a decisive overhaul of legal and political institutions. The new government abolished the feudal domains and established a centralized administrative system. It introduced modern taxation, created a national education system, standardized currency, and gave Japan a unified legal framework. These institutional changes preceded the full flowering of industrial development. In other words, the Meiji leaders understood that economic growth depends on the rule of law, secure property rights, and predictable administrative capacity.

There is a contemporary tendency to treat transformation as a matter of adopting impressive visible assets—new buildings, new hardware, new digital interfaces. But those are the last mile of a longer journey. Institutions are the invisible infrastructure that makes visible projects work. When companies go through digital transformation, they often install new systems and then discover that the real constraint lies in governance, data standards, and decision rights. When governments pursue economic reform, the binding constraint is rarely the technology itself; it is the quality of public administration. The Meiji Restoration offers a powerful corrective: get the institutional architecture right, and the applications will follow.

Education as the engine of change

If the nineteenth-century Japanese state had a singular obsession, it was education. The new government understood that a modern nation could not be run by a narrow elite alone. It needed engineers, administrators, noncommissioned officers, managers, and literate citizens who could participate in a national economy and a mass military. The system of compulsory primary education, established in the early 1870s, was not merely a social program. It was a strategic investment in the country’s ability to absorb complexity. Over time, Japan developed a cadre of professionals who could operate and improve modern systems without constant foreign supervision.

This focus on human capability is perhaps the most directly transferable lesson from 1868. Every sustained transformation—whether national, regional, or corporate—ultimately depends on people. Technology can be purchased; institutions can be legislated; but skills and habits of mind must be cultivated through deliberate educational effort. The Meiji leaders were remarkably clear that the nation’s true capital was its population. They prioritized literacy, numeracy, and practical knowledge because they knew that advanced systems would fail without disciplined operators. In our current environment of rapid automation and artificial intelligence, the same logic holds with renewed force. The countries and organizations that succeed will not be those that simply own the newest tools, but those that invest systematically in the human capacity to use them wisely.

The costs of transformation

It would be a mistake to romanticize the Meiji Restoration. It was an authoritarian undertaking, driven by a small oligarchy, and it imposed heavy costs. The push for national wealth and military strength came with harsh labor conditions, militarism, and a suppression of dissent. The rapid adoption of Western forms was accompanied by a painful reconfiguration of Japanese identity. And the eventual trajectory of Japanese militarism in the twentieth century carries a grim warning: the pursuit of national greatness can become its own pathology. Any credible account of the Meiji legacy must acknowledge this darker side.

For contemporary readers, the point is not to adopt the Meiji leaders as models of virtue. It is to recognize that transformation is never free. There are always losers, dislocations, and cultural strains. Leaders who promise change without cost are either naive or misleading. The Meiji story forces us to confront the uncomfortable fact that profound change requires sacrifice. But it also shows that sacrifice can be meaningful when it is directed toward clear goals and guided by capable institutions. The task of leadership is to manage these trade-offs honestly—sharing the burdens fairly and maintaining trust through transparency and accountability.

A lasting lesson

The Meiji Restoration remains relevant because the fundamental conditions of its success—clear-eyed threat assessment, strategic borrowing, institutional development, investment in education, and honest acknowledgment of costs—are timeless requirements for substantive change. We live in an era of unprecedented transformation, when the pace of technological and geopolitical change can feel overwhelming. Yet the temptation to respond with rhetoric, shortcuts, or imported formulas is as strong as ever. Japan’s nineteenth-century leaders knew that survival required something more demanding: a patient, disciplined effort to build the capacities that make change durable. That is a lesson not only for nations, but for every institution that aspires to navigate the future without abandoning its own foundations.

This is a lesson not just for nations, but for any organization that wants to move forward without losing its way.

Meiji Restoration and National Reformation

Within a handful of generations, Japan went from being a small, isolated island with little industrial capacity to a modern industrial state capable of defeating Russia.

While the Meiji Restoration of 1868 is often cited as a major turning point in Japanese history, I believe that it represents something much broader than simply a historical event: it is one of the best examples of how a country can intentionally reform itself in response to external pressures and rapid changes in the world.

In today's world, where governments, companies and organizations are undergoing massive transitions due to technological, demographic and geopolitical factors, I believe that studying the Meiji experience is a good idea. It reminds us that successful reform is not based on enthusiasm or slogans, but on rigorous planning, openness and the careful cultivation of capable institutions.

The Survival Concern

The restoration was a response to the threat of extinction. The Tokugawa shogunate had ruled Japan for over 200 years through a system of limited engagement with the outside world, controlling foreign trade and restricting contact with foreign powers. By the mid-19th century, the system was dangerously fragile.

As foreign countries with modern technology and imperial ambitions expanded into Japanese territory, it became clear that Japan's defense was insufficient. When Commodore Perry arrived with his "black ships" in 1853, it was obvious that the current system could no longer protect Japan. Those who overthrew the shogunate knew that the old system was no longer sustainable.

Their goal was not simply to change the government, but to preserve Japan's independence. This is important to note. The leaders of the Meiji Restoration did not set out to modernize at any cost. They began with a sober assessment of the nation's weaknesses. They knew that modernization was not an option, but a necessity to maintain national sovereignty.

Today, many organizations and countries face similar challenges. Technological disruption, supply chain crises, climate change and shifting global power dynamics can make existing systems obsolete overnight. The lesson here is not to panic or ignore the issue, but to take an honest look at the nation's shortcomings. Sustainable change begins by recognizing the gap between current capabilities and future requirements.

Strategic Borrowing, Not Imitation

One of the most intriguing aspects of the Meiji Restoration was its attitude toward foreign knowledge. The leaders did not try to copy any one country. Instead, they looked at several countries and selected features that could be adapted to Japan's circumstances.

The legal system was based on French and German models; the navy was modeled after the British navy; the educational system was influenced by American and European practices; the constitution was based on the Prussian-style strong executive. This was not blind imitation, but conscious adaptation.

The Meiji approach reflected a significant level of intellectual discipline: to treat foreign examples as resources to be assessed, not as templates to be revered. In today's world, where best practices spread quickly across borders, there is a strong tendency to copy successful innovations in their entirety—new technology platforms, management systems, or policy designs from highly successful countries. But transferring ideas without context rarely works.

What made Japan's borrowing process successful was the existence of serious institutional intermediaries—government officials, engineers, teachers, and military officers—who translated foreign ideas into practical applications. They did what we would call today's capacity building: investing in the people and institutions that would operate the new systems. The takeaway for modern leaders is simple: Foreign ideas are only useful if there is local capacity to adapt, implement, and improve them.

Institutions Before Infrastructure

There is a common misunderstanding about the Meiji Restoration, that it was about building railways, factories and telegraph lines. While the physical infrastructure was impressive, it was not the foundation. The foundation was a comprehensive overhaul of the legal and political systems.

The new government abolished the feudal domains and established a centralized government. It introduced modern taxes, established a national education system, unified the currency, and established a unified legal system. These institutional changes preceded the industrial boom.

In other words, the Meiji leaders recognized that economic growth depends on the rule of law, secure property rights and reliable government capacity. There is a temptation in today's world to think of reform as acquiring tangible assets—new facilities, new equipment, new software. But these are the last steps in a much longer process.

Institutions are the invisible infrastructure that makes tangible assets work. When companies undergo digital transformation, they often implement new technology before realizing the real challenge is governance, data standards, and decision-making power. When countries pursue economic reform, the biggest obstacle is usually not the technology itself, but the efficiency of the public sector. The Meiji Restoration teaches us a valuable lesson: set up the institutional framework first, and the rest will follow.

Education as the Driver of Change

If there was one thing the Meiji government was obsessed with, it was education. The new administration realized that a modern country could not be run by a small elite. It needed engineers, civil servants, soldiers, managers and educated citizens who could contribute to the national economy and a large military.

The compulsory primary education system introduced in the early 1870s was not just a social initiative. It was a strategic investment in the country's ability to deal with complexity. Eventually, Japan produced a class of experts who could operate and improve modern systems without needing constant foreign help.

This focus on human capital is perhaps the most directly applicable lesson from 1868. Ultimately, all long-term reform—national, regional, or corporate—depends on people. You can buy technology; you can pass laws; but you have to train skills and ways of thinking through education.

The Meiji leaders were very clear about the fact that the country's greatest resource was its people. They focused on literacy, numeracy and practical skills because they knew that advanced systems would not work without skilled operators. In our current era of rapid automation and artificial intelligence, this logic is even more important. The countries and organizations that will succeed will not be those that merely have the latest tools, but those that systematically build the human capacity to use them effectively.

The Price of Reform

It would be a mistake to see the Meiji Restoration as a positive example. It was an authoritarian process carried out by a small elite, and it came at a high price. The quest for national wealth and military power involved harsh working conditions, militarism, and the suppression of dissent.

The rapid adoption of Western models led to a painful transformation of Japanese identity. Moreover, the subsequent course of Japanese militarism in the 20th century serves as a stark warning: the pursuit of national greatness can become an obsession in itself. A full understanding of the Meiji legacy must include this darker side.

For modern observers, the message is not to emulate the Meiji leaders as moral role models. It is to realize that reform always has a price. There are always victims, disruptions, and cultural conflicts. Leaders who promise reform without a price are either naive or untrustworthy. The Meiji story forces us to accept the uncomfortable truth that major reform requires sacrifice. But it also shows that sacrifice can be worthwhile if it is directed toward clear goals and backed by capable institutions.

The challenge of governance is to manage these compromises honestly—sharing the burden fairly and maintaining public trust through transparency and accountability.

A Lasting Lesson

The Meiji Restoration remains relevant because the basic conditions for its success-realistic assessment of threats, strategic borrowing, institutional development, investment in education, and honest recognition of costs-are universal conditions for meaningful reform. We live in an era of unprecedented reform, where the pace of technological and geopolitical change can seem overwhelming. But the urge to respond with slogans, shortcuts or borrowed models is as strong as ever.

Japan's leaders in the 19th century understood that survival required something more demanding: a long-term, methodical effort to build the capabilities that make reform sustainable. This lesson applies not only to nations, but to any organization that wants to move forward into the future without losing sight of its core values.

In less than thirty years, Japan went from the fringe of the world economy to a competitor with the Russian Empire. The most important lesson to be drawn from the Meiji Restoration is perhaps its emphasis on education. In every successful transformation, there has been an investment in education. Those who are ultimately successful will not be the ones who own the latest tools, but the ones who invest in developing the skills to operate them. The Price of Change

This is not the right time to romanticize the Meiji Restoration. It was an authoritarian transformation that was implemented by a small ruling class and had negative consequences. The drive for national wealth and military power resulted in harsh working conditions, militarism and the repression of political opposition. The rapid adoption of Western-style institutions caused a painful shift in Japanese national identity. And the eventual rise of Japanese militarism in the twentieth century is a sobering reminder that the quest for national greatness can lead to self-destruction. It is vital that the Meiji legacy is not viewed through a rose-tinted lens. The point for contemporary readers is not to view the Meiji leaders as paragons of moral excellence. When looking for a model for how to strategically transform an economy or an organization, one of the clearest models is the Meiji Restoration of Japan.

Over a period of time (around 40 years or so), a small, relatively insignificant island nation became a powerful nation in its region, eventually becoming a superpower comparable to the US in terms of its economic and military power. The example of Japan is especially helpful since it demonstrates how a nation can undertake intentional, strategic change. Since we are currently in a period of global economic transformation, the Meiji Restoration serves as an excellent model for how to transform an economy and for those of us who wish to transform our organization or country.

# Strategic Borrowing, Not Imitation

Another important aspect of the Meiji Restoration was how it handled the use of foreign ideas and technologies. The leaders of the Meiji era did not seek to replicate any other foreign country. Instead, they searched out the best elements of multiple other countries and tried to build those elements into Japan. For instance, they borrowed much of the legal system from France and Germany, used British naval tactics, adopted some American educational values, and adopted a constitution that followed the pattern of Prussia with a much stronger role for the executive branch.

This illustrates a real aspect of creativity in which foreign ideas were treated as tools that could be used for a particular purpose, rather than copying another country entirely. In our world today, in which technological advances, software innovations, and many other forms of development happen extremely quickly across national borders, it is tempting to think of copying what other countries do. When someone has a very successful company, it is tempting to try and implement their strategy for success, whether that be a new set of technology, a new methodology, or a particular policy. Rarely will such an approach work.

What made the ability of Japan to borrow foreign knowledge so effective is that there were also institutions that could translate that knowledge into domestic practice. Examples of these institutions are schools, universities, government agencies, businesses, and military units. These institutions had the capacity to take foreign knowledge and apply it in the context of Japanese society. The Meiji leaders understood that, in addition to importing knowledge, there also had to be those who could understand the knowledge and know how to use it. These people were essential to developing what we might now call capacity-building. This is the process of creating the skills and abilities needed to carry out the new system.

Today, we can see that foreign knowledge is very useful, but it is only as good as the local ability to use it. Organizations that seek to transform themselves will benefit from realizing that they should use foreign knowledge as a source of knowledge, rather than a source to copy.

The Meiji leaders viewed the need for reform as a question of survival. They were aware that Japan needed to change its situation in order to avoid being swallowed up by the West. This was not because they wanted to imitate Western countries, but because they feared Japan’s vulnerability to Western imperialism and expansionism.

Prior to the mid-19th century, Japan had been kept virtually isolated from the rest of the world through a ban on overseas trade. This isolationism was enforced by the Tokugawa daimyos, who controlled most of the country.

However, by the latter half of the 19th century, the tendency of Japan to remain isolated started to crumble. Foreign countries started to make demands for Japanese access to their own markets and territory. This culminated in the voyage of Commodore Matthew Perry (USS Californian), who brought an American fleet to Japan in 1853, warning Japan that it must open itself to foreign expansion.

The Meiji leaders believed that Japan must be saved from this threat. In so doing, they had to choose a path of drastic reform to save the country. Thus, the Meiji leaders began to implement drastic reforms in response to what they felt was an existential threat to the security of Japan. This is a detail that is often missed by those who talk about the history of the Meiji period.

Similarly, the Meiji leaders intuitively understood that Japan’s survival was threatened. It was not enough just to try to modernize; it was essential to ensure that modernization happened fast enough to keep Japan out of the hands of Western imperialists. At the time, many countries in the West were actively trying to expand their empires, and Japan was one of these empires’ targets.

Today, we can see that countries and organizations today face similar threats. Supply chain disruptions due to climate change, economic downturns caused by geopolitical changes, and advancements in technology and weapons systems all present threats that the Meiji leaders had to contend with. This similarity makes studying the Meiji Restoration relevant to us today.

# The foundation of institutional reform

A common misunderstanding of the Meiji Restoration is that it focused on creating new physical infrastructure such as roads, ports, railways, factories, and telegraph lines. While there was indeed a great deal of physical infrastructure created during this time period, this was built upon something that was missing entirely: the ability to manage and sustain the infrastructure. Essentially, the Meiji leaders recognized that a functioning infrastructure requires a legal system, property rights, and governance capacity that makes running the infrastructure possible.

In the modern day, there is a tendency to equate transformation with the creation of new things, such as buildings, technologies, or other innovations. However, these are just the final phases of a much longer process. What makes all other parts of the process workable are the underlying systems and processes.

Digital transformation in business organizations often results in the implementation of new technologies, while ignoring the underlying business processes or organizational culture, which may cause difficulties. Economic reforms in governments usually suffer from inadequate governmental administrative competencies, rather than the inability to develop new technologies. The lesson from the Meiji period is that the foundations need to be created first; if they are created properly, everything else will easily follow.

Education was one of the major concerns of the Meiji government in the 19th century. It is clear that a modern country cannot run itself through a small elite. Rather than just modern technology, the newly modernized country would need scientists, bureaucrats, non-commissioned officers, business managers, and a populous with the ability to operate a large-scale modern economy. Also, the modernized country needed soldiers who were able to fight and work together effectively in a larger-scale army. In 1872, compulsory primary education was established by the government. This can be seen as a social measure, but the primary aim was to create a modern workforce.

As a result, Japan would not need to remain dependent on the West for industrialization and development. One lesson of the Meiji period is that all of the necessary measures for any kind of transformation are related to human capital. Every transformation involves building a new workforce, policy-makers, or institutions. Any transformation will have to involve human beings who understand the new systems.

We need to be wary of glorifying the Meiji Restoration. It was driven by a military dictatorship and it had a huge cost. To establish Japan’s wealth and military strength, national policies had to promote harsh working conditions, militarism, and suppression and oppression of ethnic minorities. The cost of Westernization imposed on the Japanese people the psychological pain of being forced to leave their cultural identity behind and become westernized.

In addition to being dangerous to other States, Japanese imperialism of the 20th century told the story of a country whose obsession with expanding its power and influence at the expense of other countries ultimately resulted in disaster. Therefore, no study of the Meiji period can avoid turning the page to these negative elements.

The implications of the Meiji experience are not that we should admire them as praiseworthy leaders, nor that they are role models that we should become. Transformation always comes with pain and suffering. Anyone who promises you change without pain is simply a liar or ignorant. The Meiji period demonstrates that change costs something – whatever the cost is. However, you can pay it if you know how and make a plan. One of the most important challenges is to quantify and internalize the cost of change. And, importantly, you must make sure that the cost of transformation is shared across the organization.

The significance of the Meiji period remains because the fundamentals of change – accurate assessment of the threat, strategic adoption of other models, establishing the institutional mechanisms of change, investing in education, and understanding the pain that comes with change – remain fundamental to change of any size. Living through periods of disruptive technological change and rapid geopolitical shifts may seem unmanageable, but the need for broad and simplistic solutions to complex problems today are as pervasive as ever.

The founders of Meiji-era Japan realized that the foundation for survival was the arduous and sustained effort to create the skills necessary to survive indefinitely.

From an obscure island nation situated on the fringe of the world to an influential world power in decades, Japan came through the Meiji restoration of 1868 with flying colors. On top of this, it won a war against Russia. We tend to discuss the Meiji restoration as being the defining event in Japanese history. But it represents an excellent case study of how countries respond to internationally generated threats and change. It proves that our countries can adapt to a changing world.

Today our world is accelerating in terms of global change. Nations, institutions, and industries are being forced to respond to changing circumstances including technological improvements, population shifts, and changing geopolitics. The Meiji restoration represents a successful example of how to engage in effective transformation.

The Meiji restoration teaches us that transformation is not about enthusiasm and slogans alone. Transformation requires an organized approach and responsibility to build the necessary institutions.

Survival and Change

Japan came into the Meiji restoration with a fear of decline.

For many years, Japan was kept isolated from the rest of the world during the Tokugawa shogunate period. Traditionally, foreigners could only enter in specific ports. By the mid-1800s this situation was unsustainable.

Nations with high levels of industrial and technological capabilities made numerous attempts at forcing Japan to open it’s doors. American Commodore Matthew Perry demonstrated the inability of Japan to defend itself with his “Black Ships” in 1853. The people who brought about the downfall of the Tokugawa regime were aware that, without change, Japan could no longer exist as an independent country. The Meiji leaders sought to protect Japan’s sovereignty as they restructured the government.

Given that we live in an era in which change is often unavoidable, there is little debate regarding the necessity of transformation. Countries and corporations understand that they must change in order to remain relevant. Whether the change is due to technological advancements, geopolitical shifts, or climate change, the fact that transformation is required cannot be denied. The importance of recognizing weakness in a society that is undergoing major transformation is paramount. Many countries fail to recognize vulnerability when initiating the transformation process.

Adopting but not copying overseas ideas

One feature of the Meiji Restoration that might be examined in the present day is how Japan utilized foreign concepts. The Meiji group did not simply duplicate any individual country’s form of governance. On the other hand, they studied other countries and selected the components of each system best suited to Japan. The court system of the Japanese government was modeled after France, the military was modeled after Britain, and the constitution was modeled after Prussia.

While the idea of simply copying foreign ideas may appear simplistic, it was a calculated process. The leaders of Japan did not seek to copy foreign ideas entirely. Instead, they examined various concepts for their potential to be modified and adapted for use in Japan.

As the world becomes increasingly connected and ideas become easier to transfer internationally, it is tempting to simply adopt a foreign concept without modification. However, adopting a foreign idea before testing its relevance to your own setting will surely lead to failure.

Adoption requires adaptation. In the early years of the Meiji period, this meant that the Japanese sought out foreign experts to assist Japan in developing the capacity for operating the new ideas. The most significant lesson for leaders today is that they should actively seek out foreign experts and utilize foreign knowledge in combination with local knowledge.

Focusing on institutions rather than infrastructure

It is frequently misunderstood that the focus of the Meiji Restoration was on constructing railways and factories. Although there were indeed a number of large-scale infrastructure developments during the Meiji period, the focus was not on infrastructure. The focus was on transforming the nation’s institutional and legal framework. The new government dismantled the feudal system in favor of a centralized national government. This included replacing the feudal tax system with a modern tax system, creating a national education system, establishing a unified currency, and developing a legal system based on modern law.

This transformation took place long before Japan itself became fully industrialized. The reason for this timing was that industrial development does not only rely on access to capital and material resources; it also depends on the rule of law and the protection of property rights, which are institutional characteristics.

In today's world, most people focus on the material components of production—the factories, machines, computers, etc.—as they relate to economic and social change. However, the physical components will not work effectively unless they are accompanied by a supportive institutional environment. Many companies have failed to transform successfully because they have concentrated on digitizing their product systems and implementing sophisticated IT solutions while ignoring the need to re-engineer their business models.

Similarly, governments often embark on significant social change programs to bring about rapid technological growth, only to find that the limitations lie not with the available technology, but with managerial capacity. Governments must ensure that they first establish the correct institutional framework before expecting the benefits of technological growth. When the framework is established, individual companies can prosper and governments can achieve sustained economic expansion.

The role of education in bringing about change

Without the remarkable growth in human capital that the new government achieved in Japan, the Meiji restoration would not have met its goals. Compulsory education was introduced in 1872. Through compulsory education, the Japanese government was investing in the development of skilled workers and teachers. The Japanese government wanted to prepare its citizens not only to be productive employees, but to be active participants in a modern economy.

The leaders of the Meiji government recognized that human capital growth was essential for the success of Japan's development. To effectively build a country that could develop on its own, the leaders of the Meiji government had to focus on training. An increasing pool of skilled workers and qualified teachers provided the opportunity for Japan to continue to develop and to adjust as its economy shifted toward industrialization.

From the Meiji experience, we can learn that human capital growth is essential for any country today that wants to survive. The need for human capital growth is also even greater considering the challenges facing us today. In a world driven by data and artificial intelligence, a government’s ability to respond to crisis is not driven solely by its technological base. A government’s ability to respond to crisis is also determined by its ability to train its workforce to be able to use sophisticated tools.

The leaders of the Meiji era should teach the benefit of training workers for a modern economy. To succeed in the economic challenges facing us today, countries will need to undertake significant training efforts.

The costs of transformation

It would be a mistake to view the Meiji restoration in a straightforward way. The Meiji restoration was authoritarian. It led to a powerful elite headed by the Meiji leaders. It had casualties. Workers suffered from poor working conditions. There was militarism. Dissenting voices were suppressed. There was a painful shift in Japanese identity as the country embraced Western customs. And there was a senior leadership that eventually led the country into a path of militarism during the first two decades of the 20th century.

The Meiji restoration is not a clean story of progress. In order to discuss the legacy of the Meiji restoration according to current understanding, we must acknowledge these negative aspects.

It would be incorrect to use the Meiji leaders as examples for our own actions. However, it is important to remember that transformation comes with a cost. Some people will always lose out. Some people will be negatively impacted by the transition. There will always be discord when societies change. Those leaders who say they can change the world without any pain are either lying to themselves, or secretly deceiving their followers.

Beyond this, however, there is another lesson from the Meiji history that we should learn: suffering. A transformation, if there is one, will involve great costs. We can't deny that. However, we can also understand that people are willing to take risks if they understand why, and if they believe their efforts will yield positive results. These factors mean that we must take in the costs of transformation seriously. We need to allocate the burden of transformation equitably and must clearly communicate our intentions and how we'll carry them out.

The lesson of the Meiji restoration

Though it's no longer relevant today, the Meiji restoration represents a blueprint for successful modernization that is still important: assessing threats objectively, adopting useful ideas from other countries, reforming institutions, building an educational system, and being transparent about the costs involved. We live in a time of immense change, where changes in technology and geopolitics can seem overwhelming. Currently, there is also a risk of people trying to solve problems with simplistic approaches, slogans and short-lived solutions. The leaders of Meiji-era Japan realized that survival required more than slogans: it required careful, long-term efforts to build the kinds of capacity needed for successful change.

To understand the character and meaning of this service we must look to the Lord Himself, whose actions show us what it is, and whose words tell us what it means. “He gave thanks,” we are told in the Gospels. The service is eucharistic, for this thanksgiving preceded the breaking of the bread and the giving of the cup. St. Luke and St. Paul imply that He gave thanks before He handed over the cup, but Matthew and Mark expressly say so. CAIUS JULIUS CAESAR OCTAVIANUS, commonly known as Augustus, the first Roman emperor, lived at the time of the birth of Jesus Christ. He was born in Rome in 62 B.C. and died in A.D. 14. He received the title of Augustus from the senate in 27 B.C. as a token of gratitude for the restoration of certain privileges which had previously been withheld from the legislative body. All of his successors adopted this title. He was a member of the gens Octavia and the son of Caius Octavius, a praetor. He was the grand-nephew of Caius Julius Caesar and was named the principal heir in the latter's will. After the assassination of Julius Caesar, the young Octavianus went to Rome to claim his inheritance. Although he initially aligned himself with the republican party, he ultimately formed a coalition with Mark Antony. He was very popular and, in defiance of the wishes of the Senate, he successfully secured the consulate in 43 B.C. That same year, he made an agreement with Antony and Lepidus, thereby establishing the Second Triumvirate (tresviri reipublicae constituendae). The three men agreed to govern the affairs of Rome for a period of five years. The Roman dominions were divided such that Lepidus received Spain, Antony received Gaul, and Augustus received Africa, Sicily, and Sardinia. The first coordinated military action of the Triumvirate was directed against Caesar's assassins and the Senate's faction, which was led by Brutus and Cassius. These forces suffered a decisive defeat at the Battle of Philippi in 42 B.C., after which the fate of Rome rested effectively in the hands of two men. Lepidus, who had consistently been treated with neglect, attempted to seize Sicily for himself. However, Augustus quickly won over Lepidus's troops. Upon his submission, Lepidus was sent to Rome, where he spent the remainder of his life serving as pontifex maximus.

This project seeks to enhance the responsiveness of health services to the needs of communities in the North Queensland region. The project is guided by the research question: How can integrated place-based planning be best developed and implemented to address the unique contexts of northern Queensland? This study is important because investing in the health workforce and improving models of care is a strong economic pillar for sustained prosperity. A healthy community is a prerequisite for stable local populations, which in turn enables continued regional economic development. While northern Australia shares common health challenges and service delivery characteristics (small, dispersed populations in challenging geographies), there is a lack of coordination in planning and delivering health services from community to primary and hospital care, resulting in inefficiencies, duplication, service gaps and suboptimal health and economic outcomes. This project presents a unique opportunity to bring together health industry partners and engage with local communities to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of service planning and delivery. The study is conducted in two phases. Phase 1 involved synthesis and spatial mapping of existing publicly available data to create the Northern Queensland Health Atlas. This online interactive map visually displays population and health data, available health services and workforce information. Users can select and overlay indicators to visualise unmet needs or gaps in services and workforce to facilitate informed consideration of these issues. The Atlas can be explored here. A gap analysis was also undertaken to establish a broad understanding of unmet health needs in the project region. Aim of the Research

The aim of this project is to improve the responsiveness of health services in the North Queensland region of Australia to better respond to the needs of the local communities. The question this study addresses is: ‘How can integrated place-based planning best be developed and implemented in place-based frames to address the unique context of northern Queensland?’

Why is this question important?

Investing in the health workforce and improving models of care is a robust economic pillar for continued prosperity. A healthy community is a prerequisite for a stable population in a locality, which enables continued regional economic development.

While northern Australia has common health challenges and common health service delivery (small, dispersed populations across challenging geographies), there is a lack of integration and coordination in the planning and delivery of health services from community to primary through to hospital care. This leads to inefficiencies, duplications, gaps in services, and utilisation of services when they are not optimally utilised with minimal positive health and economic outcomes.

This Project brings together the unique opportunity to unite health industry partners and engage with communities to improve the efficiency of service planning and delivery for health services in the region.

Methods

The study was conducted in two phases. Phase 1 followed with the synthesis and spatial mapping of existing publicly available data that resulted in the development of the Northern Queensland Health Atlas. This interactive, online map contains visualises available health service and workforce data and population and health data. Places and areas on the map can be selected and indicators overlaid to visually display and consider unmet needs or gaps in services and workforce. This Atlas can be explored here.

Furthermore, a gap analysis was undertaken to establish a broad understanding of the unmet health needs in the project region. A pragmatic approach, guided by key principles regarding health care equity, was adopted in developing a composite Index of Unmet Need that incorporated indicators of known health determinants, current and projected health needs, service needs, workforce and geographical access. This project produced the Gap Analysis of Health Needs and Services in the Northern Queensland Region Report, which can be requested.

The Atlas and Gap Analysis guided the stakeholders in consultation to prioritise community for engagement in place-based health planning processes in Phase Two. Further consultations with local stakeholders in these prioritised areas will facilitate co-selection of 3-4 communities to participate in place-based health planning processes in Phase Two. Place-based planning will involve the co-design, implementation and evaluation of new or modified models of care with the communities. The impacts and outcomes of the Project will be evaluated in relation to quality of care, efficiency, service provider and consumer satisfaction, and acceptability and sustainability of the processes.

The project’s goals are to enhance existing regional responsiveness to localised needs in the North Queensland region. It will address the following problem: how to best develop and implement integrated place-based planning to suit the diverse local contexts in northern Queensland. This project is critical given that investment in a skilled health workforce and improved models of care is one of the most powerful levers for economic gains to support sustainable prosperity. A healthy community is essential for a stable population and enabling continued regional economic development.

In South Korea, functional, active-ingredient based skincare is a staple in consumers’ daily skincare routine, suggesting that the demand for such products is unlikely to shift anytime soon. This is an attractive opportunity for SKINMADE, as in 2025, South Korea’s cosmetics market was valued at USD 18.4 billion and is expected to reach USD 31.1 billion by 2035 (Expert Market Research, 2026). Thus, the Korean cosmetics market is especially attractive to SKINMADE, given its large market size and growth potential beyond its current Malaysian market.

Beyond South Korea’s domestic market, facial skincare also dominates the global K-beauty products category, representing around 60% of the USD 17.27 billion global K-beauty products market in 2026 (MarkNtel Advisors, 2026). This reinforces that skincare, rather than colour cosmetics or other product categories, is where both domestic and international demand for Korean-origin beauty products is concentrated, further supporting SKINMADE’s decision to lead with an active-ingredient skincare portfolio rather than a broader beauty range.

On the other hand, the Korean market presents a considerable amount of competition, because Korean consumers are well familiarized with skincare products and will not necessarily choose an imported brand just because it is foreign. Rather, they will assess the brand against existing, well-established Korean competitors by comparing factors like formulation, efficacy of ingredients, and technical credibility. In a study of Chinese cosmetics brands’ competitiveness in the Korean market, Jin and Chang (2026) found that foreign entrants cannot rely solely on brand origin or general appeal to gain a competitive advantage, and instead need to strengthen their brand value and technical competitiveness to compete effectively in Korea’s mature and highly competitive cosmetics market. Although this finding was drawn specifically from the Chinese cosmetics context, the same underlying logic plausibly extends to other foreign entrants, including SKINMADE, given that Korean consumers generally evaluate brands on formulation credibility rather than country-of-origin appeal alone.

Therefore, SKINMADE cannot depend on the foreignness of its brand as the sole source of differentiation when it enters the Korean market. Instead, to establish a competitive edge, the brand would need to demonstrate the efficacy of its active-ingredient portfolio, defend its active concentration levels, and provide sufficient substantiation of its clinical claims. In short, if SKINMADE was to succeed in the Korean market, it would not simply be because of its foreignness, but rather because it could prove the formulation of its products could meet the high quality and performance standards of Korean consumers.

At the beginning of The Big Oil, we see a short history of how oil has been produced and consumed and how it relates to global politics. We see old archival footage of documentaries produced by public broadcasting networks, with images that include graphs and charts that show us what percentages of the world’s oil production are derived from OPEC countries. But this is merely a lead-in to the film’s main point: that The Big Oil is intended to prove that wars and other violent political conflicts are created and sustained by those who control the production and consumption of oil.

Examples of wars mentioned by the political analysts who speak in The Big Oil include the one in Sudan, Kuwait, and between Iran and Iraq—also a conflict described in the film as being related to oil. These types of wars aren’t accidental. The analysts also say, in response to a question that could be interpreted as asking about the oil industry in Iraq, that “the Iraq war has everything to do with oil production and consumption.” They say, in effect, absent an actual question, that it’s common knowledge that U.S. foreign policy generally, and the Iraq war specifically, are driven by the American need to control oil flows in order to meet the increasing demand of consumers for oil. This level of global oil consumption can only be met if the oil industry is able to sell this commodity while maintaining a price that is affordable enough for the general population. Volume can only continue at that price level if the industry continues to make money, even though the public gets the benefit of low gasoline prices, among other things, as a result. According to the film, any U.S. politician who won’t risk telling the American public that our current oil crisis, which has started us down the path of war, is dangerous would simply have no hope of being elected. But if he told people that they would have to deal with that reality, then he’d be jeopardizing the oil industry. That in turn would have disastrous consequences for the U.S. economy and for the American way of life. As a result, the film concludes, the government is lying to us. And it is at war to prepare that lie.

The Materia Medica is a collection of drug provings, made by Hahnemann and his disciples on healthy persons, and, as at present existing, is chiefly a formal record of the subjective and objective symptoms observed by the provers or their associates. With few exceptions it does not attempt to trace the pathological connection between the symptoms, to give a physiological explanation of them, or to distinguish between the characteristic and generic symptoms. It is given in plain untechnical language, as it would be given by an intelligent but uninstructed patient, leaving the physician to trace the connections and formulate the explanations. It is a record of facts in the vernacular, and will remain intelligible as long as the language endures. But Hahnemann had a much higher conception of the Materia Medica knowledge which the physician needs than this simple presentation implies. In his essay “The Power of Small Doses,” in Hufeland’s Journal, he describes this knowledge as consisting in knowing which organs the drug deranges functionally, how it modifies other functions of the body, which nerves it principally benumbs or excites, what alterations it effects in the circulation and digestion, in the mind and disposition, in the secretions, in the muscular fiber, how long it acts, and by what means it is rendered powerless. Why did Hahnemann not construct his Materia Medica on this model? The answer is, that his remarkable sagacity, combined with his brilliant genius and prodigious learning, earned him the title of “double-headed prodigy” from Jean Paul Richter. He clearly perceived that the positive facts essential for the construction of a Materia Medica are the observations of the prover, recorded in plain unfigurative and non-hypothetical language; that the comprehensive construction he deemed desirable must result from the application of the sciences of Physiology and Pathology to these facts; and that the facts of the proving, being based on positive observation, are enduring and unchangeable. On the other hand, he saw that the sciences of Physiology and Pathology are incomplete and progressive, and are undergoing continual change, and that their terms and their significance vary as the theories on which they are based change. A Materia Medica constructed by combining these two elements, one constant and the other variable, would necessarily be transient. It would soon become obsolete, and in its decline would obscure the constant element, and the labor of the provers would be lost to the world. It would be an intermingling of the current theories of physiology with the facts of observation. The precise point and extent of the intermingling would in time become indistinguishable, and a vitiated record would be transmitted to posterity, which the advance of science would soon render useless. A comparison of the present state of Physiology with that of 1800, when even the very terms were nearly obsolete, will show the profound wisdom of this view. On the other hand, the pure records of observed facts, untainted by theoretical speculations, are in our possession pure, intelligible, and available as when first recorded by the Master.

I get some very interesting emails from time to time, and today was no exception. I got an email from “M”, and when I read it, I called “M” and asked him if I could publish it. I thought it was important to do so, especially after I published Egor Prosvirnin’s “Appeal”, which some readers took as anti-German and accused me of being anti-German myself. As I explained later, I was trying to point out the growing anger toward Germany in Russia. I don’t share that anger myself, but I think it is legitimate, if not justified. I soon noticed that the most vocal and hostile protests against that post did not come from Germans or German sympathizers, but from the same group of neo-Nazis who consider the defense of anything German to be part of their ethos. Nevertheless, I felt uneasy about the whole episode. Contrary to some assumptions, I am not anti-German, nor do I believe in collective or inherited guilt. As an anti-Soviet Russian, I understand the difficult position of those who oppose their current regime while at the same time recognizing their own people as victims. Many countries and nationalities are still resentful and angry toward Russians, especially for what Soviet forces did during World War II. I think that resentment is legitimate, even if it is sometimes historically one-sided. It is always difficult to be the target of such anger, whether it is fully deserved or not. So, when I got “M”’s email, I decided to share it with you. I am grateful to “M” for giving me permission to do so.

The reversible potential of the fuel cell decreases with increasing current. This is because of the losses in the fuel cell. The losses in the fuel cell are due to three factors: activation, ohmic resistance and concentration. The fuel cell performance curve is used to study the fuel cell. The performance curve is a graph of the voltage versus the current. The output current depends on the active area of the fuel cell. Therefore, to compare the fuel cells of different sizes, the current density is used instead of the current. The current density is the ratio of the current to the surface area of the fuel cell (Ebrahimi et al., 2022). When hydrogen and oxygen molecules penetrate the catalyst surface, a certain amount of energy is required to start the reaction. This energy is called the activation energy. To provide this energy, a part of the fuel cell voltage is consumed. The electrochemical reactions occur and the voltage drop occurs across the anode and cathode catalysts. This voltage drop is called the activation drop. The activation loss is largely independent of the current density. The hydrogen oxidation reaction at the anode catalyst produces electrons and protons. These electrons and protons must reach the cathode catalyst to start the reduction reaction. Protons are conducted through the membrane and electrons are conducted through the electrodes and the external circuit. The resistance to the transfer of charged species in the polymer fuel cell components causes a voltage reduction. This voltage reduction is expressed as the ohmic (resistance) drop. The resistance loss increases linearly with increasing current density. The voltage drop due to the species concentration usually occurs at high current densities. When a large current is drawn from the fuel cell, the reaction rate at the catalyst sites increases. Therefore, the reactant species must move through the porous electrode medium at high speeds to reach the reaction sites. However, as the species pass through the porous medium, their pressure and concentration decrease. This leads to a sharp decrease in the species concentration at the catalyst. This causes a significant voltage drop in the polymer fuel cell at high current densities. In the case where the species transfer rate equals the species reaction rate and the species do not accumulate in the catalyst, a limit current density is established. The fuel cell's current density cannot exceed this value. To determine the output voltage of the fuel cell, first, the reversible voltage must be calculated and then the losses mentioned above must be subtracted (Ebrahimi et al., 2022).

Therese Graf’s portrait has changed meaning since it was taken, probably while she sat on a bench in front of her house near Lake Starnberg. At the moment of exposure, it captured an inconsequential and random instant in the life of a woman who, by conventional historical standards, had little agency beyond her immediate local environment. As a depiction of an individual in a specific setting, the photograph documents a person, a moment, and a place as they existed at that precise point in time. On the surface, its indexicality seems self-evident: Oskar Maria Graf certainly did not need to be reminded of his mother’s existence. But the further temporal and spatial distance grows from the moment of exposure—through the subsequent history of exile and into the present—the more abstract the photograph’s significance becomes. In the context of “strong history,” it serves as visual evidence not only of existence but of the experiences of a particular social stratum, a generation, and the passage of time. It becomes a robust indicator of migration history rather than a mere illustration. This historical narrative is embodied not only in the face of the aging woman but also in the itinerary and perception of the photograph itself, both as an image and as a physical object. Just as the wrinkles on her face bear the traces of her lifespan, the photograph remains a trace of her existence. As a material object, once displayed on a wall in New York City and now preserved in an archive box in Munich (fig. 8), the portrait narrates a journey characterized by loss and change. Through this trajectory, Therese Graf’s portrait became entangled with the histories of modernity and migration, thereby attaining global agency. Ultimately, the photograph illustrates the capacity of images to constitute “strong histories” of migration.

长期以来，火山学在公共传播方面一直面临一个难题：公众对火山喷发的想象往往高度同质化——烟雾弥漫，岩浆喷涌，爆炸声震耳欲聋。仿佛每座火山都是一颗等待引爆的炸弹。这种“爆炸中心论”的误解不仅扭曲了火山过程的真实面貌，也在一定程度上影响了灾害认知和防灾策略的制定。

事实上，火山喷发的风格并非单一，而是沿着一个从宁静溢流到剧烈爆炸的连续谱系分布。而塑造这一谱系的核心变量是岩浆的物理化学性质，而非火山本身的规模或高度。

要澄清这一误解，首先必须区分火山喷发的两种基本机制：岩浆喷发和潜热喷发。前者以熔融岩石从地壳深部上涌、减压、脱气并涌出地表为特征；后者则涉及地下水与热岩层接触后急剧汽化而产生的蒸汽爆炸。即便同在岩浆喷发范围内，喷发方式也截然不同。

夏威夷式喷发以低黏度玄武质岩浆为物质基础，挥发分含量低、气体容易逃逸，因此表现为持续而温和的熔岩喷泉与熔岩流，而非摧毁性的爆炸。冰岛裂隙式喷发则沿张性断裂带中长有六公里的裂缝同时出露，形成大范围熔岩覆盖，改变地形却极少伴随爆炸冲击。与之相对，普林尼式喷发则以高硅质流纹岩或安山岩岩浆为特征，黏度高、挥发分难以逸出，气体过饱和后在上升通道内急剧膨胀，最终产生高达数十公里的火山灰柱和碎屑涌浪。1991年皮纳图博火山即为典型：其喷发物以浮石和火山灰为主，而非液体熔岩流；爆炸的能量来自岩浆内部溶解气体的迅速释放，而非某种“地下炸弹”的预先存在。

进一步看，公众常将“火山喷发”与“全球性灾难”直接关联，忽视了喷发风格受控于岩浆储库状态、围岩应力、通道形态等系统参数。黏度不仅决定气体的逃逸速度，也决定了岩浆上升过程中是否存在自生震动。低黏度玄武岩可以在几小时内沿裂隙铺展数十平方公里，过程可预测且适应性强；而高黏度岩浆则在上升过程中频繁凝固堵塞，压力重新积累，从而形成间歇性爆炸。因此，同一座火山在不同时期也可能切换喷发模式。例如，全球火山活动数据库显示，许多复式火山在历史时期有过溢流式与爆炸式的交替纪录，这取决于每次岩浆补给中SiO₂含量的波动及含水矿物的存在。换言之，喷发风格是动态的，并非火山“本质”所固定。

从灾害管理角度看，挑战这一误解具有实际意义。若决策者与公众仅以爆炸式喷发为模板，就可能低估溢流式喷发对基础设施的缓慢破坏——熔岩流虽不致命，却能吞没道路、农田和定居点，且难以用常规爆破方式改道。反之，若以溢流为唯一预期，则会在高黏度岩浆突然发生水蒸气爆炸或火山碎屑流时措手不及。因此，火山学家强调“喷发场景”而非“喷发类型”，要求在监测数据（地震活动、地表形变、气体通量）基础上动态评估喷发风险，而不是依赖刻板印象中的火山形象。

此外，认识喷发风格谱系还有助于理解火山与环境的复杂关系。溢流式喷发释放大量二氧化碳和二氧化硫，但短期内可能引起区域冷却而非全球气候“惩罚”；爆炸式喷发则将硫酸盐气溶胶注入平流层，对气候的扰动更显著。这种差异再次表明，火山现象不能以单一刻板概念简单概括。

综上，火山学的核心方法之一，就是破除“所有火山都是爆炸式”的直觉偏见，转向对物质属性和过程机制的精细分析。喷发风格是岩浆黏度、挥发分、通道几何以及外部水体共同作用的产物，而非某种固有“脾气”。唯有在学术研究与公共沟通中同时坚持这种多元性，才能避免误解的循环，也才能在真实灾害来临时，区分警报的等级与措辞的轻重。火山并非地球的定时炸弹，而是一台受控于物理化学条件的释放系统；它可能咆哮，也可能低语，而科学家的任务，正是听懂每一种语言。

长期以来，火山学在公共传播方面一直面临着一个问题：公众对火山喷发的想象往往过于单一——黑烟滚滚，岩浆喷涌，爆炸声震耳欲聋，仿佛每座火山都是一颗等待引爆的炸弹。这种“爆炸中心论”的误解不仅扭曲了火山活动的真实面貌，也影响了灾害认知和防灾决策。

事实上，火山喷发的风格并非千篇一律，而是沿着一个从平静溢流到剧烈爆炸的连续谱系分布。决定这一谱系的关键因素是岩浆的物理化学性质，而非火山的体积或高度。

要澄清这种误解，首先要区分两种基本的喷发机制：岩浆喷发和蒸汽喷发。前者涉及岩浆从地壳深处上升、减压、脱气并最终喷出地表；后者则源于地下水与热岩相互作用导致的快速汽化。即使在岩浆喷发的范畴内，喷发方式也各不相同。

夏威夷式喷发以低粘度玄武岩岩浆为物质基础，挥发分含量低，气体易于逸出，因此表现为持续的熔岩喷泉和熔岩流，而非破坏性的爆炸。冰岛裂隙式喷发则表现为长达数公里的裂缝沿拉张断裂带同时打开，形成大面积的熔岩覆盖，改变地形，却很少伴随爆炸冲击。

相比之下，普林尼式喷发则以高粘度流纹岩或安山岩岩浆为特征，挥发分难以逸出，气体在上升管道内过饱和后迅速膨胀，最终形成高达数十公里的火山灰柱和碎屑流。1991年皮纳图博火山的喷发物质主要是浮石和火山灰，而非液态熔岩流；爆炸的能量源于岩浆内部溶解气体的快速释放，而非预先存在的“地下炸弹”。

进一步来看，公众往往将“火山喷发”与“全球灾难”直接联系起来，而忽视了喷发风格受岩浆库状态、围岩应力、通道几何形状等系统参数控制。粘度不仅影响气体逃逸速率，还影响岩浆上升过程中是否发生自震。低粘度玄武岩可在数小时内沿裂缝延伸数十平方公里，过程可预测且适应性强；而高粘度岩浆在上升过程中频繁凝固堵塞，导致压力再次积聚，引发间歇性爆炸。因此，同一座火山在不同时期也可能发生喷发模式的切换。

在公共讨论中，人们通常会形成关于火山爆发的刻板印象，认为它们会产生巨大的烟柱，喷射熔岩，发出震耳欲聋的轰鸣声，就像悬而未决的炸弹一样。这种关于“爆炸性的”理解不仅误导了公众对火山自然灾害的理解，还影响了灾害预防和减轻措施的形成。

然而，一种爆发类型并非仅存在于爆发中。爆发类型实际上而变化。它们存在于一个指数式的区间当中。它们并不取决于火山的尺寸或位置，而是取决于岩浆本身的特性。

在我们深入了解这个问题之前，我们应该记住一个基本的原理：并非每种类型的爆发都能用岩浆解释。事实上，每种类型的爆发都仅仅代表了一种特定的事件。然而，即使岩浆类型相同，爆发类型也可能不同。

例如，夏威夷的爆发几乎总是由液体玄武岩岩浆流出，由于其挥发分含量极低而不会发生爆炸。因为它们避免了爆炸，所以它们永远不会积累压力。相反，它们表现为地表上的快速喷涌和熔岩流。相比之下，冰岛的爆发表现为由巨大的熔岩源沿6000公里的断层线喷发的熔岩流，它可以重塑地貌，但爆发本身往往很小。

普雷尼式（维苏威式）爆发则由火山熔岩组成，其中富含非挥发分，使其难以喷发。这些岩浆通常具有高的非挥发分含量和更粘稠的灶况。由于熔融岩浆的非挥发分含量的积累，岩浆被压力释放拉动出地壳并向上移动。它们随着高度的增加而急剧膨胀。这会产生高达20-30公里高的火山灰流和火山碎屑流，以及可能时速超过100公里的火山碎屑流。

例如，1991年皮纳图博火山爆发主要由火山灰和火山渣穹顶组成；它几乎没有表现出熔岩流。皮纳图博的炸是由岩浆性质ではなく产生压力的膨胀导致的。

人们通常将火山爆发视为巨大的全球灾难。此外，人们倾向于认为差点引起灾难的爆发将是剧烈的。然而，人们并未表现出对差异的考虑，这些差异包括火山类型和喷发类型。然而，所有这些特征都与岩浆的性质相关联。岩浆的粘度决定了挥发分释放的速率，以及爆发过程中可能的地震。即使在地震中，如果岩浆从裂缝中流动，可以形成数公里长，持续数天。然而，高粘度的岩浆会不断阻止流入，造成压力积累，导致火山活动。即使同一天也能看到爆发能量的差异。例如，许多活跃火山中喷发的潜伏爆发序列在世界上已有几百年被盗录。这被认为与岩浆中的硅和含水量有关，后者与硅含量成比例。简而言之，爆发类型并不是火山的固有性质，而是爆发事件中时间和空间的关系。

对于减轻而言，优化这种理解可能存在。如果我们坚持用爆发模式进行指导，我们可能会忽视最需要关注的现象：持续的、循序渐进的威胁，不像爆发那样剧烈，但随着时间的推移会逐渐侵蚀我们的基础并污染我们的资源。如果我们认为火山会爆发，我们最终将被其他潜在的灾难所困扰，例如火山灰。因此，我们应该指导预想和评估的爆发模式。“我们应该确定官方的爆发类型并关联数等级，并确定所有必要的计划和演习，并制定计划：任何发生的基础上，因为公众不应盲目认为爆发是大规模的。”“我的建议应该与公众的教育宣传有关：我们必须确定并告知公众，每个地区、每种类型的火山都有独特的爆发特性。”“我认为这是理解当地 Measure 必须的。”

最后：我认为我们应该摆脱这种普遍的误解。我们得到的结果可能会更好。安危所有居民和国家的福祉。这项研究是至关重要的，因为不止我们能做，科学家们，火山只是火山，所以重要的是我们寻求为公众提供可通过爆发性灾害进行宣传的信息。

The first reading is from the prophet Ezekiel. It describes how God brings life to those in the grave. God says that He will raise up the dead of Israel and bring them back to their land. This is how they will know that He is God. God will put His spirit in them. This is an allusion to the resurrection of Christ. Jesus was crucified, died, and was buried. But He rose from the dead (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Matthew 27:50-54 describes how the dead came out of the graves and went into Jerusalem. It must have been scary to see. But it was not like “The Walking Dead” on TV. This fulfilled the foreshadowing in the first reading. God promised to raise up the dead of Israel so that they would know that He is God. Ironically, in Matthew 27:54, the centurion and those with him said, “Truly this man was God’s son.” God is the one who restores life to us, both spiritually and physically.

This research explores the potential of Service Design in the field of education, specifically in the area of Education for Sustainable Development (ESD). ESD is a significant area of transformation in the educational system, yet it has a limited presence of Service Design and knowledge. This research, based on grounded theory and contextualised in English primary education institutions, identifies Service Design as a strategic approach to support transformational change in institutions seeking to adopt ESD. A literature review was conducted on Service Design, the vision of ESD and its application in English schools. The review connected the capacity of Service Design to redesign services at the organisational level with the gap in normative re-educative change processes towards ESD in English schools. Building on these findings, the research conducted in-depth case studies of five primary schools, followed by a cross-case analysis, to understand ESD change at the organisational level, focusing on elements relevant to normative re-educative change processes, i.e. social and personal norms and values embedded in organisational systems. From the case studies, specific principles, concepts and processes were identified that enable schools to engage with ESD at a profound level. The knowledge from the case studies was further developed to relate the ESD phenomenon to Service Design. Applying service thinking and organisational change theory, a Sustainable Education as a Service Model (SES Model) was developed to conceptualise ESD as a phenomenon within a service system. The SES Model was presented to the Service Design community for validation. Sense-making of ESD was undertaken through semi-structured interviews with seven service design practitioners, who explored the SES Model. The results of the interviews indicated that the model enhances service designers’ capacity to engage with ESD. The application of the model demonstrated that designers could envision its use at the level of normative re-educative change. This research establishes ESD as a relevant and novel concept for Service Design, offering significant opportunities for further research and practical application.

This research explores the potential of Service Design in the field of education. Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) in education is a significant area of transformation in educational systems. However, at present ESD has limited representation of Service Design and associated knowledge. Grounded in grounded theory and situated in English primary education institutions, this research identifies Service Design as an approach that helps to facilitate transformational change in institutions seeking to adopt ESD. A literature review on the topic of Service Design in education, vision of ESD and ESD in English schools was conducted. The literature review connected the capability of Service Design to redesign services at the organisational level to gaps that exist in normative re-educative change processes toward ESD in English schools. Building on initial findings, this research was anchored by in-depth case studies of five primary schools and cross-case analysis, to understand ESD change at the organisational level – focusing on elements relevant to normative re-educative change processes of social and personal norms and values embedded within organisational systems. From the case studies, specific principles, concepts and processes were identified that enable a school to engage with ESD at a profound level. The knowledge from the case studies was developed further, to relate the ESD phenomenon with Service Design. Applying service thinking and organisational change theory, a Sustainable Education as a Service Model (SES Model) was developed, which conceptualised ESD as a phenomenon in a service system. The SES Model was presented to the Service Design community for validation. Sense making of ESD was undertaken by semi-structured interviews with seven service design practitioners who explored the SES Model. The results of the interviewees suggested the SES Model enhanced their capacity to engage with ESD. The application of the SES Model also suggested that designers could envisage how to use it at the level of normative re-educative change. Consequentially, this research provides ESD as a relevant new concept for Service Design with significant opportunities for further research and practice.

However, at the same time, Service Design is at the present very much the norm in relation to ESD, with very little knowledge of it. This research utilised grounded theory and the English institutions of primary education in order to identify Service Design as a strategic approach to facilitating craft of transformational change in institutions to engage with ESD. The literature review identified knowledge in Service Design, the General concept of the vision of ESD and how it is applied in English schools in order to connect Service Design's capacity to redesign services at its organisational level with the gap in the normative re-educative change processes towards ESD in English schools. On the basis of this, the following then were developed to understand ESD change at organisational level with in-depth case studies of five primary schools: social and personal norms or values embedded into organisational systems that are relevant for normative re-educative change processes. From these case studies, that are connected to organisational normative re-educative change processes, particular principles, concepts and processes were identified that enable schools to engage with ESD at the extremely profound level. The knowledge emanating from the case studies developed further to relate ESD to Service Design. The Sustainable Education as a Service Model (SES Model), through the application of service thinking and organisational change theory was developed to conceptualise ESD as a phenomenon at Service System level. The SES Model has been presented to Service Design community for validation from which Sense Making of ESD was undertaken through semi-structured interviews of seven service design practitioners with the SES Model. The results from the interviews showed an enhancement in Service Designers' capacity to engage with ESD. Service Designer's application as to where they can see ESD at the level of normative re-educative change was demonstrated. ESD concept was further established as a relevant and novel concept to which Service Design can draw upon and add greater knowledge to Service Design thinking. The research therefore can present significant opportunities for further research and application.

This research investigates the potential of Service Design in education with an emphasis on education for sustainable development as an important area of transformation in education. Education for sustainable development has too little presence of Service Design and knowledge. Based on a grounded theory and grounded in English primary schools in England, it identifies Service Design as the way to enable transformational change in learning institutions aspiring to take action for education for sustainable development. Following a literature review of the Service Design and the vision of education for sustainable development and its use in English schools the research explores the capacity of Service Design to re-design services at the organisational level relative to the gap of a normative re-educative change process towards education for sustainable development in English schools. Following on from these findings the research carries out in-depth case studies of five primary schools followed by a cross case analysis in an attempt to understand change at the organisational level in relation to education for sustainable development, specifically the elements of a normative re-educative change process relating to the social and personal norms and values system embedded in organisational systems. From the case studies principles, concepts and processes that enable schools to engage in education for sustainable development at a deeper level were identified and related to the phenomenon of education for sustainable development with Service Design using a sustainable education as a service model. Service thinking and applied change theory at an organisational level were used to understand education for sustainable development as a phenomenon within a service system to develop a sustainable education as a service model. The sustainable education as a service model was then presented to the Service Design community for validation enabling sense-making of education for sustainable development to be undertaken through interviewing seven service design practitioners in semi-structure interviews and exploring the model. The results of the interviews with the service design indicated that an education for sustainable development model could increase service designers capacity to engage in education for sustainable development. Sensible use of the model in service design showed that designers see themselves using service design for education for sustainable development at the level of normative re-educative change. Education for Sustainable Development has been identified as a relevant and new concept in Service Design and has immense opportunity for further research and use.
